tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
schema.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:

1	# SPARK Night 2026: the adaptive care challenge
2	
3	**What this is.** One working document for the Beyond Next Ventures challenge at SPARK Night (13-14 Nov 2026, Ashoka University). It was written in stages during the night of 13 November. Internal to the team.
4	
5	**Status, 13 Nov 2026, about 11:10 PM.** Complete. All parts A to M are in this file. Three claims checks re-opened the sources of about 183 load-bearing facts, and their corrections are applied throughout. Part M says what was not checked and what was not found.
6	
7	**How to trust a number here.** Every number traces to a fact ID in `research_notes\dtx\` (for example D1-01-F02), where its source link, date and status are recorded. Numbers were read at source by one research agent; the load-bearing ones were then re-checked by a second, and corrections are applied in the text. Anything seen only in a search summary is marked "search summary only". Mock-up screens show example data only.
8	
9	**The challenge, as set by the fund.**
10	
11	> We need ways to manage chronic disease burden at scale despite limited access to resources, specialists and irregular clinical follow-ups. Patients need treatment methods that responds to their specific condition, and will remain adaptive to patient needs between appointments. How can digital therapeutics use rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers to continuously personalise care, thereby bringing measurable improvements in health outcomes to patients who cannot access frequent specialist support? The opportunity is to extend effective treatment into everyday life, beyond monitoring and reminders.
12	
13	**Contents**
14	
15	<!-- CONTENTS -->
16

1	## A. Read this first
2	
3	### The answer in six lines
4	
5	1. **What the fund is asking for.** Care that changes the treatment itself between appointments, from a device or biomarker reading, for people who cannot see a specialist often. Part B decodes the wording.
6	2. **What the evidence says.** Outcomes move when a home reading leads to a changed treatment. They mostly do not when the reading is only shown or a reminder is sent. Self-monitoring of blood pressure alone moved pressure by 1.0 mmHg; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling) it moved 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05]. An independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication [D1-01-F39]. Part D has the trials, including the ones that failed.
7	3. **Where India's gap is.** The government's hypertension programme controls pressure well in patients who come back, and about half do not come back [D1-03-F10]. In its first nine districts 21.2% of people with high blood pressure are controlled [D1-01-F11]. Parts C, C2 and D2.
8	4. **What to build tonight.** A home blood-pressure step loop: a checked home reading, the state's published step protocol run from a data file, a question on whether the medicine was taken, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Part J is the build pack.
9	5. **Who else does it.** No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings (a search result, not proof of absence). The nearest products abroad are a Japanese cuff maker's UK software that drafts a medication plan for the clinician (search summary only) [D3-06-F35] and US programmes that use their own clinicians [D1-05-F1]. A UK company that dosed one blood-pressure medicine by app was wound up in April 2026 [D3-06-F07]. Parts F1 and H.
10	6. **Who you are pitching to.** The mentor's fund led a 2023 round in Wellthy, an Indian digital-therapeutics company, and its first investment in 2015 was the Japanese company whose blood-pressure app is covered by insurance there [D3-06-F01, D3-06-F26]. That app coaches lifestyle and does not change medicines [D3-06-F19]. Your loop is the step neither had. Part K.
11	
12	### What you can say at noon, and what you cannot
13	
14	| You can say | You cannot say |
15	|---|---|
16	| Every branch of two published protocols passes our tests. | The product is safe, validated or approved. |
17	| A simulation of ours, built on the programme's own figures, shows where the gain would come from. | The loop improves control. No patient has used it. |
18	| Readings from teammates flowed end to end, and this share passed the quality check. | These are clinical data. |
19	| A doctor approves every change; the software only drafts. | The software prescribes or treats. |
20	| It is a student prototype, not a medical device. | It complies with any rule. India's July 2026 guidance treats such software as a device [D2-04-F01, D2-04-F07]. |
21	
22	### The three weak spots to own before someone else raises them
23	
24	1. **Who pays.** Our price of ₹149 a patient a month is an ASSUMPTION. Public-sector medicines cost about ₹200 a patient a year [D2-01-F12]. At our price the US$100 million-a-year test fails in India alone (part F2).
25	2. **It will be regulated**, and a study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first [D2-04-F13, D2-04-F14].
26	3. **An Indian trial of software for clinicians found nothing** [D1-01-F46]. The loop must earn its value between visits, among the patients who do not return.
27	
28	### Which part to read
29	
30	| If you are | Read |
31	|---|---|
32	| Building the engine and screens | J, then E |
33	| Building the hardware | J (hardware plan and test), then E (sensing and reading quality) |
34	| The biology student | D, D2, then J (protocol files and test cases) |
35	| Leading the pitch | A, K, L, then G and I |
36	| Writing the one-page thesis | J (the draft), B (the argument), C (the numbers) |
37	| Asked "who else is doing this" | F1 and H |
38	| Asked "how big is it" or "is it legal" | F2 |
39	
40	### How far to trust this document
41	
42	- **Every fact carries an ID that links to its source.** Part M has the register: what each note recorded, the link, whether the page was opened or only seen in a search summary, and the verdict of the claims check where one was run.
43	- **Three kinds of statement are ours, and marked so:** OUR VIEW (a judgement), OUR ARITHMETIC or OUR ESTIMATE (a sum or a guess from stated inputs), and ASSUMPTION (an input we chose). The option scores, the market model, the simulation and the price are all ours.
44	- **Mock-up screens show example data.** Every name and reading in them is invented.
45	- **What was not done:** no customer interviews; no measured split of public and private treatment; no current specialist counts; no Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps was found. Each part ends with what it could not find.
46	- **It is not medical or legal advice.** The legal sections say what the texts say and list the questions for a lawyer.

1	## Decision brief: what to build tonight
2	
3	*Written 13 Nov 2026, about 10 PM, from the six Round 1 research notes. Updated about 10:30 PM after the clinical claims check: 53 claims re-opened at source, 48 confirmed, 5 tightened in wording, none wrong (`research_notes\dtx\D3-01 Claims check - clinical evidence.md`). The India and market facts were checked next (about 45 claims: 29 confirmed, 7 corrected, 5 contested, 3 not found; `D3-02 Claims check - India and market.md`), and the corrections that touch this brief are applied below.*
4	
5	![The difference between monitoring and a therapy loop](adaptive-care-pictures/00-the-loop.png)
6	
7	*Diagram: monitoring stops at the reading; a therapy loop sends the reading back as a changed treatment.*
8	
9	### What the evidence says
10	
11	1. **Programmes that change the medicine from home readings work.**
12	   - UK trial TASMIN-SR (552 patients): patients adjusting their own dose by a set plan lowered systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg more than usual care at 12 months (D1-01-F02).
13	   - US trial HyperLink (450 patients): pharmacists adjusting drugs from home readings got 57.2% controlled against 30.0% (D1-01-F04).
14	   - Rural China (33,995 people, 326 villages): village health workers starting and stepping doses by protocol got 57.0% under 130/80 against 19.9% at 18 months. After 4 years, cardiovascular events were lower (hazard ratio 0.75 at age 60 and over, 0.64 under 60), with no difference in falls, low pressure or kidney outcomes (D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38). The programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid village doctors for results, so the protocol is not the only cause.
15	2. **Monitoring and reminders alone do not.**
16	   - Self-monitoring alone, pooled across trials: 1.0 mmHg, no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling): 6.1 mmHg (D1-01-F05).
17	   - A reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 patients): 0.5 mmHg, not significant (D1-01-F06).
18	   - Tuberculosis pillbox trackers (ASCENT, 23,483 patients): no improvement in outcomes (D1-02-F59).
19	   - An independent US review (Peterson Health Technology Institute, October 2024) found that only programmes which adjust medication give clinically meaningful falls in pressure (D1-01-F39).
20	3. **The pattern repeats in other diseases.**
21	   - Warfarin: patients who test at home and change their own dose had fewer clots (risk ratio 0.47) and fewer deaths (0.55). Those who tested at home and phoned the clinic had no fewer deaths (0.94). Each group was compared with usual care, not with the other (D1-02-F05).
22	   - Insulin in type 2 diabetes: a device that computes the next dose cut HbA1c by 1.0 point against 0.3 (D1-01-F13).
23	   - Heart failure: stepping drugs up fast after discharge, with four clinic visits in two months, cut death or readmission at 180 days to an adjusted 15.2% against 23.3%, with more side effects reported (41% against 29%) (D1-01-F27). Two large trials of telemonitoring that left treatment to the usual clinicians or to nurse protocols found no benefit (D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33).
24	4. **India's gap is the dose change and the return visit.**
25	   - Government hypertension programme, 21,895 patients: 51% came back for follow-up. Among those who did, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group (D1-03-F10).
26	   - Tamil Nadu household survey, 6,856 adults: over 95% of diagnosed patients are on treatment, yet control rates were 9.8% for diabetes and 35.4% for hypertension (D1-03-F09). The claims check notes that the paper's summary does not state the denominator for the two control figures.
27	   - Rural community health centres had 79.9% of required posts in four specialities unfilled, as of March 2023 (D1-03-F16). A primary-care consultation lasted about 2 minutes in studies from 2013-2015 (D1-03-F24).
28	5. **Nobody in India was found running a dose-change loop from home readings.** The diabetes programmes sell a sensor plus doctor and coach (D1-04-F02, D1-04-F03, D1-04-F04, D1-04-F05, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07). The protocol model in the government's open-source app stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step logic was found in it (D1-06-F40). Phable, the best-known home blood-pressure app, shut in February 2023 (D1-04-F23).
29	6. **Why earlier companies died.** Pear Therapeutics sold its assets for about US$6 million against US$130 million of liabilities (D1-02-F42). Akili earned US$523,000 from prescription sales in 2023 (D1-02-F44). Teva withdrew its sensor inhaler in June 2024 (D1-02-F41). They sold apps or sensors without a payer, and users leave fast: across 93 mental-health apps, the median share still using the app at day 30 was 3.3% (D1-02-F26).
30	
31	### The caution to carry
32	
33	An Indian trial already tested software for clinicians and found nothing. mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 patients) gave nurses and doctors a decision-support app during visits; the difference from well-run usual care was 0.98 mmHg, not significant (D1-01-F46). So the value must come from changing the dose between visits and reaching the half who never return. A prompt at a visit that was happening anyway adds nothing.
34	
35	### Scores
36	
37	Two gates first: the product must change the therapy itself from device or biomarker feedback, and it must be buildable honestly tonight. Then six axes, scored 1 to 5. Weights: proof 25, market 20, feasibility tonight 20, gap 15, deep-tech 10, low risk 10.
38	
39	| Option | Proof | Market | Tonight | Gap | Deep-tech | Low risk | Score |
40	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
41	| Home blood-pressure step loop | 5 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 4 | **4.35** |
42	| Insulin dose guidance, type 2 diabetes | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3.35 |
43	| Adaptive home rehabilitation (camera and pulse) | 3 | 3 | 5 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3.35 |
44	| Heart-failure dose loop | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 3.10 |

55	### The three to weigh
56	
57	**1. Home blood-pressure step loop (recommended).**
58	- *What it is.* A home cuff reading goes into an engine that runs India's own published step protocol: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, with a re-check every 30 days, lab values checked before telmisartan is raised, and referral rules for very high readings, abnormal lab values and pregnancy, including women of childbearing age not on effective contraception; the sheet covers adults over 30 (Gujarat protocol, D1-06-F14). The engine proposes the next step. A doctor approves in one tap. The patient gets the change in their own language.
59	- *Why.* The strongest proof of any option, including deaths and strokes avoided at scale by non-physicians. The largest patient pool: 35.5% of Indian adults aged 20 and over have high blood pressure (D1-03-F01). The exact Indian protocol text is public. No Indian service was found.
60	- *Noon demo.* A live reading, the proposal, the approval, the patient message.
61	- *Honest test results.* Every branch of two published protocols passes. A simulated cohort built on the programme's own control-by-step figures from 159,292 patients (D1-06-F04), labelled as a simulation. Reading-quality tests on teammates.
62	- *Main risk.* It can look like "just rules", and the mWellcare result will be raised. The answer: the rules are what the trials show works; nobody runs them at home; the hard parts are trusting a home reading, checking the pills were taken before raising a dose, and proving safety. Who pays is the open business question.
63	
64	**2. Insulin dose guidance for type 2 diabetes.** Strong trials and pharma interest. But no open type 2 simulator exists (D1-06-F30), so tonight's test would be thin, and low blood sugar is a real hazard. Sanofi already has a dosing app (D1-04-F09). Best shown as the second protocol on the same engine, tested on paper.
65	
66	**3. Adaptive home rehabilitation.** The easiest demo. But software rehabilitation only matches in-person care and does not beat usual care (D1-02-F07, D1-02-F54), and Lupin says it already holds an Indian Class C device licence for cardiac rehabilitation (D1-04-F15).
67	
68	*Also weighed.* Heart failure has strong outcome proof and fits "far from a specialist" best, but it needs lab values, so it cannot be tested honestly tonight; it is the later protocol for the same engine. The breathing plan has the most hardware and the best open data, but the dose change that works in asthma needs no sensor and sensor inhalers failed commercially. Warfarin has the best proof and a small market. Weight-loss injection support is a hot market with no outcome evidence yet and three Indian players already in.
69	
70	### Recommendation
71	
72	Build option 1. Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion.
73	
74	- **Software:** the protocol engine, the patient chat, the doctor's approval screen, the test harness.
75	- **Hardware:** read the cuff (a phone photo of any cuff's screen, with the person confirming the digits; typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand), and build a small clip with a motion sensor that checks arm position and stillness, so a bad reading never triggers a dose change.
76	- **Biology:** encode the protocol and its safety branches, write the test cases, own the clinical story.

38	### B4. The loop: sense, decide, confirm, act, learn
39	
40	Five stages: what happens at each, and where existing products stop.
41	
42	![Monitoring against a therapy loop](adaptive-care-pictures/00-the-loop.png)
43	
44	*Diagram: monitoring stops at the reading; a therapy loop changes the treatment.*
45	
46	- **Sense.** A home device gives a number, valid only if taken correctly. Level 1 products stop here (B3).
47	- **Decide.** Software applies a written protocol to this patient's readings and proposes the next step. Coaching apps decide advice, not doses [D1-04-F04]; the protocol model of the government's Simple app stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step ladder was found in it [D1-06-F40].
48	- **Confirm.** A doctor, nurse or health worker approves each change; unsafe cases go to a specialist. Trials used pharmacists [D1-01-F04] or village doctors [D1-01-F09]; no Indian service doing this from home readings was found [D1-04-F09].
49	- **Act.** The patient gets the new dose, medicine or exercise level. Heart-failure telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol found no benefit (B6).
50	- **Learn.** The next readings show whether it worked, and the loop runs again. At 24 government-programme sites, 10,621 of 21,895 patients did not return [D1-03-F10].
51	
52	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: India lacks decide, confirm and act between visits.

68	### B6. Five rules the evidence gives
69	
70	OUR VIEW: five rules, each with the numbers behind it.
71	
72	**1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring alone lowered systolic pressure 1.0 mmHg against usual care, no effect; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, 6.1 [D1-01-F05]. Two US heart-failure trials of remote monitoring without a mandated dose protocol (1,653 and 1,437 patients, 180 days) found no benefit [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33]. Fast dose stepping after discharge cut readmission or death (B7) [D1-01-F27]. Against usual care, warfarin patients who set their own dose from home tests had fewer deaths (risk ratio 0.55, 8 trials); in 3 separate trials, those who left the dose to the clinic did not (0.94); the two approaches were not compared head to head [D1-02-F05].
73	
74	**2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In a UK trial (1,182 patients, 12 months), sending readings electronically added a non-significant 1.2 mmHg over paper once the family doctor adjusted doses [D1-01-F03]. In rural China (33,995 people, 18 months), supervised village doctors stepping drugs by protocol got 57.0% under 130/80, against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. At 4 years cardiovascular events were lower (hazard ratio 0.75 at age 60 and over), though the programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid incentives [D1-01-F38].
75	
76	**The Indian null result belongs here.** mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension or diabetes, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: no Indian randomised trial tested that (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
77	
78	**3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children gave 84% adherence against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.
79	
80	**4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Apps and sensors sold on their own failed. Pear's assets fetched just over $6 million against $130 million of liabilities (2023-2024) [D1-02-F42]; Teva stopped US distribution of its sensor inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41]. Those at scale are paid by employers and insurers for clinician-led programmes (Hinge Health: revenue $234.970 million in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16]) or sell a therapy device (Insulet: $842.0 million [D1-05-F41]).
81	
82	**5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In 8 remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants) median retention was 5.5 days. Clinician referral added 40 days [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.
83	
84	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: B10 turns these rules into a test for any idea.

114	### B9. Terms used in this document
115	
116	- **Adaptive depth:** 0-4 score for how far a product changes treatment.
117	- **Adherence:** taking the medicine as prescribed.
118	- **Closed loop:** a device that measures and adjusts therapy itself.
119	- **Digital therapeutic:** software that changes one patient's treatment.
120	- **Endpoint:** the result a trial is judged on.
121	- **Hazard ratio:** a risk ratio measured over time; below 1 means fewer events.
122	- **HbA1c:** blood test of average sugar over about three months.
123	- **INR:** clotting test that sets the warfarin dose.
124	- **Not significant:** small enough to be chance (a null result).
125	- **Protocol:** a written step-by-step treatment plan.
126	- **Randomised trial:** people get treatments by chance.
127	- **Risk ratio:** risk with treatment divided by risk without; below 1 means lower risk.
128	- **Systolic:** the upper blood-pressure number, in mmHg (millimetres of mercury).
129	- **Time in range:** share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL.
130	- **Titration:** stepping a dose towards a target.
131	
132	### B10. So what for us
133	
134	OUR VIEW. Any idea must pass three questions.
135	
136	1. **What changes?** After a home reading the prescription is different (level 4), within days.
137	2. **Who decides?** A general doctor, nurse or health worker, under a written protocol; unsafe cases go to a specialist.
138	3. **What moves, and who pays?** One endpoint passes an accepted threshold in 90 days, and a named payer wants it.

33	### C3. The care cascade
34	
35	![Share of adults with high blood pressure who know, are treated and are controlled, 2018-19 and 2023-24](adaptive-care-pictures/22-india-cascade.png)
36	
37	*Chart: in the first nine districts of India's hypertension programme, 21.2% of adults with high blood pressure were under control in 2023-24, up from 14.5% in 2018-19 [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11].*
38	
39	A care cascade follows people with a condition through four steps: has it, knows it, is treated, is controlled. Percentages compare only when the denominator (the group the percentage is taken of) is the same, and several sources do not state it clearly.
40	
41	#### High blood pressure
42	
43	| Source | Aware or diagnosed | Treated | Controlled | Denominator | Status |
44	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
45	| NFHS-5 district paper, 2019-21 [D1-03-F05] | 46.0% (district average; range 6.1-89.6%) | 18.7% | Not used: the abstract gives 32.9% "of individuals with hypertension", which cannot sit above 18.7% treated; the preprint below gives 9.1% of all for the same 2019-21 survey [D1-03-F07] | Contested; do not read this row as one chain | Abstract opened |
46	| NFHS-5 preprint, 1.69 million adults, 2019-21 [D1-03-F07] | 36.7% (about 1 in 3) | 17.7% (under 1 in 5) | 9.1% (about 1 in 11) | All people with hypertension | Preprint; record opened |

52	The same survey gives 73.7% controlled when only people aged 15-49 on drugs are counted, and 9.1% (about 1 in 11) when everyone with hypertension is counted; the ages and denominators differ, so the two do not compare [D1-03-F06, D1-03-F07]. 54	#### Diabetes
55	
56	- **Undiagnosed:** 43%, about 38.6 million, in 2024 [D1-03-F28].
57	- **Treated but not controlled:** in Tamil Nadu over 95% of diagnosed people were treated, yet the diabetes control rate was 9.8% (the abstract does not state the denominator) [D1-03-F09].
58	- **Slow insulin starts:** a mean of 7 years of diabetes before insulin in one older Indian study (search summary only) [D1-03-F30]. 60	OUR VIEW. So what for us: two steps leak, diagnosis and control. The step from "treated" to "controlled" depends on the dose being raised and the medicine being taken, which is the decision our loop prepares.

62	### C4. Treatment is not control
63	
64	Three Indian data sets show that getting people onto medicine is not enough, and that people who return do far better than those who do not.
65	
66	**Tamil Nadu survey.** The state's doorstep programme, Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, was surveyed in 6,856 adults aged 30+ across all 38 districts (paper abstract, 2025; a South First news report gives 6,809) [D1-03-F09]. Screening reached 79.4% for diabetes and 82.6% for hypertension, and over 95% of diagnosed people were on treatment. Control rates remained low: 9.8% for diabetes and 35.4% for hypertension; the abstract does not say whether these are shares of everyone with the disease, the diagnosed or the treated [D1-03-F09].
67	
68	**India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) cohort.** A government programme with a fixed drug protocol. The cohort registered 21,895 patients at 24 sites in Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Telangana (Jan 2018-Jun 2019), followed up Jul-Sep 2019, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
69	- Only 11,274 (51%) returned [D1-03-F10].
70	- Among returners, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% [D1-03-F10].
71	- Control was 70.4% in primary care against 52.2% in secondary care [D1-03-F10].
72	- Protocol drugs: amlodipine, telmisartan or losartan, chlorthalidone or hydrochlorothiazide; 44.6% were on amlodipine 5 mg alone at follow-up [D1-03-F11].
73	
74	**IHCI district surveys.** Before and after, same nine districts, no comparison districts [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11, D1-03-F12]:
75	
76	| | 2018-19 | 2023-24 | Change |
77	|---|---|---|---|
78	| People with hypertension | 7,047 | 7,324 | |
79	| Aware | 52.4% [D1-01-F10] | 58.5% [D1-03-F12] | +6.1 points (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
80	| Treated | 40.8% [D1-01-F10] | 44.7% [D1-03-F12] | +3.9 points (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
81	| Controlled | 14.5% [D1-01-F10] | 21.2% [D1-01-F11] | +6.7 points [D1-03-F12] |
82	
83	**Return visits.** About 27% of registered IHCI patients did not return in Jan-Mar 2021 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13]. IHCI enrolled about 4 million patients, about 12.5% of the estimated total, by around 2022 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13]. Pooled Indian non-adherence to BP drugs is 48%, with a prediction interval of 9-90% (search summary only) [D1-03-F44].
84	
85	OUR VIEW. So what for us: our loop must reach the half who do not come back, between visits.
86	
87	### C5. The specialist and time gap
88	
89	Few specialists work where most patients live, and doctors who see chronic patients have very little time per visit.
90	
91	**Rural community health centre (CHC) specialist posts, March 2023** [D1-03-F16]:
92	
93	| Specialty | Shortfall | Share of required posts |
94	|---|---|---|
95	| Surgeon | 4,578 | 83.3% [D1-03-F16] |
96	| Physician | 4,499 | 81.9% [D1-03-F16] |
97	| Paediatrician | 4,425 | 80.5% [D1-03-F16] |
98	| Obstetrician-gynaecologist | 4,078 | 74.2% [D1-03-F16] |
99	| All four | 17,551 of 21,964 (4,413 in post) | 79.9% [D1-03-F16] |
100	
101	The article's rows sum to 17,580, not 17,551 [D1-03-F16]. The shortfall has stayed near 17,500 since 2014-15 [D1-03-F17].
102	
103	**Specialist counts.** The only figures are from a 2017 parliamentary committee (search summary only): about 4,000 cardiologists, 1,200 nephrologists and 650 endocrinologists, against the committee's estimated needs of 88,000, 40,000 and 28,000 [D1-03-F18]. The government told Parliament it does not hold speciality-wise doctor data (news report of the reply, 13 Apr 2025) [D3-07-F22].
104	
105	**Consultation length.** Indian primary-care visits lasted about 2.3 minutes (2013, stopwatch, 412 visits) and 2 minutes (2015) [D1-03-F24].
106	
107	**Doctor ratio and its caveat.** The government gave 1:811 in Rajya Sabha (about 2 Dec 2025), counting 13,88,185 allopathic doctors plus 7,51,768 AYUSH practitioners (traditional medicine) and "assuming that 80 per cent" are available [D1-03-F40]. Allopathic doctors alone give a lower ratio. OUR ARITHMETIC from the note: 13,88,185 x 0.8 = about 11.1 lakh, about 0.79 per 1,000 people if the population is about 1.4 billion (an assumption, not sourced) [D1-03-F40].
108	
109	OUR VIEW. So what for us: a two-minute visit has no time to read two weeks of home readings. Software should prepare the next protocol step for a general doctor or nurse to approve, with the specialist owning the protocol.
110	
111	### C6. Cost and follow-up
112	
113	Families pay a large share of health costs themselves, and the share rose in the latest year on record.
114	
115	- **Out-of-pocket share:** 39.4% of total health expenditure in 2021-22 and 43.41% in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts released 27 May 2026, via a news report) [D1-03-F23]. In 2022-23 household spending rose by ₹26,375 crore while government spending fell by nearly ₹49,000 crore [D1-03-F23].
116	- **Per visit:** medicines were 61.15% of spend per outpatient spell in a Delhi report; another report says median outpatient spend is zero (search summary only) [D1-03-F49].
117	- **Cheaper medicines:** 18,646 Jan Aushadhi Kendras (generic medicine shops), Feb 2026, priced 50-80% below branded [D1-03-F20].
118	- **Diabetes spend:** about US$109.5 per person and over US$9.8 billion in total (IDF 2024) [D1-03-F28].
119	
120	NOT FOUND: household cost per chronic-care visit; travel distance and lost wages; the share of chronic patients who see a doctor each year; loss to follow-up outside IHCI; how long a dose change is delayed, in months.
121	
122	OUR VIEW. So what for us: avoided trips save patients money, but without a rupee figure per visit we cannot yet claim a saving.
123

171	### C10. Heart failure in India
172	
173	No national count of heart failure was found, and the estimates differ widely: 1.3 to 4.6 million cases in a 2010 estimate built from disease-specific figures, whose authors say no surveillance exists (quoted in a 2024 review) [D3-07-F24], against about 8 to 10 million, about 1% of the population, in a 2016 review of local and global studies (search summary only) [D3-07-F25]. For stroke, the Global Burden of Disease study put India's prevalent cases at 9.4 million in 2021, up from 4.4 million in 1990, with over 1.25 million new cases a year (press report quoting the authors) [D3-07-F26]. The registries show patients leave hospital on too few of the drugs that work and stop them afterwards. The three guideline classes are beta blocker, RAS blocker (ACE inhibitor or ARB) and MRA.
174	
175	| Registry | Who | Treatment finding | Outcome | Source |
176	|---|---|---|---|---|
177	| National Heart Failure Registry | 10,851 acute patients, 53 hospitals, 21 states | 47.5% of eligible patients received guideline drugs | 90-day death 14.2%; 1-year death 22.1% | [D1-01-F47, D1-01-F48] |
178	| Indian College of Cardiology registry | 5,182 acute patients, 17 centres, 2019-2021 | All three classes taken: 18.8% of men, 15.9% of women | 1-year death 18.1% | [D1-01-F49] |
179	| Trivandrum, Kerala | 1,205 admissions, 16 hospitals, 2013 | 25% of weak-pump patients discharged on all three | 5-year death 59% | [D1-01-F35] |
180	| NORIN-STEMI, Delhi | Heart-attack patients with weak pumping | MRA use fell from 69% at discharge to 6% at 1 year | | [D1-01-F50] |
181	
182	The national registries differ (47.5% against about 17%) partly because one counts prescription and the other adherence [D1-01-F49]. None reports doses as a share of target [D1-01-F35, D1-01-F47, D1-01-F49].
183	
184	OUR VIEW. So what for us: a clear dose gap with high death rates, but safe titration needs lab values, so heart failure is a later protocol for the same engine.

186	### C11. What we could not find
187	
188	- Current counts of endocrinologists, cardiologists, nephrologists, chest physicians and physiotherapists.
189	- Doctors per 1,000 people, rural against urban.
190	- A heart-failure count newer than 2016; a stroke-survivor count from a primary source.
191	- Depression prevalence after 2015-16 from a primary source; a depression-only treatment gap.
192	- Share of chronic patients who see a doctor each year; loss to follow-up outside IHCI; HbA1c at insulin start in India; delay to dose change in months.
193	- Household cost per chronic-care visit; distance and wage-loss figures.
194	- Official WhatsApp India users; unique smartphone users from a regulator.
195	- Japan's 2023-24 hypertension control rate; a dated WHO India NCD death share.
196	
197	### C12. So what for us
198	
199	OUR VIEW.
200	- **Blood pressure first.** 35.5% of adults 20+, against 11.4% for diabetes on the same survey [D1-03-F01].
201	- **The leak is after treatment starts.** Over 95% of diagnosed Tamil Nadu patients are treated, yet the hypertension control rate was 35.4% (denominator not stated) [D1-03-F09]. Screening already runs at crore scale [D1-03-F20].
202	- **The return visit is the bottleneck.** 51% of IHCI patients returned, and among those who returned control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10]. The pilot endpoint is control at 90 days among people who would not have come back.
203	- **Prescriber time is scarce.** About 80% of required rural CHC posts in four specialities (surgeon, physician, obstetrician-gynaecologist, paediatrician) were unfilled in March 2023 [D1-03-F16], and visits lasted about two minutes in 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24]. Software drafts the step; a clinician approves it.
204	- **Reach needs shared phones and health workers.** 57.4% of rural women own a phone [D1-03-F42].

1	## C2. What patients and doctors say in public
2	
3	### What this part is and is not
4	
5	The team has done no interviews, so this part stands in until it does. It reports published interview studies, surveys, public app reviews and posts, labelled PUBLISHED STUDY, PUBLIC REVIEW or FORUM POST. None of it is customer evidence gathered by the team; reviews are self-selected and studies were read as abstracts only.
6	
7	### Why patients miss follow-up and stop medicines
8	
9	Eight Indian interview studies (PUBLISHED STUDY) name the same causes: feeling well, cost, family duties, fear of long-term drugs, traditional medicine.
10	
11	| Where | People | Barriers, in the authors' words |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| Coastal Karnataka, tertiary hospital | 32 hypertensive patients lost to follow-up | "symptom-driven healthcare seeking, medication non-adherence, occupational responsibilities, and competing family priorities"; wage loss, rushed consultations [D3-04-F01] |
14	| Rural Tamil Nadu (Thiruvallur) | 15 adults with diabetes or hypertension | Stopping is structural, unintentional (work, travel, caregiving) or intentional, "perceived harm, symptoms or treatment need"; "Family relationships could both support and hinder medication-taking" [D3-04-F02] |
15	| Tehri, Uttarakhand | 40 (20 diabetes, 20 hypertension) | "the use of alternative medicine"; "lack of self-management guidance from their physicians" [D3-04-F03] |
16	| West Garo Hills, Meghalaya | 52 (providers, health workers, community) | "concern about long-term treatment"; "a preference for traditional medicine constrained screening efforts"; elders decide [D3-04-F12, D3-04-F48] |
17	| Rural Meghalaya | 29 women aged 60+ with diabetes | "caregiving roles as barriers to care"; "feelings of guilt due to financial dependency" [D3-04-F04] |
18	| Rural Punjab | 8 focus groups plus 15 health professionals | "beliefs in alternative therapies, drug side effects"; "Physicians' guidance and support were motivating them" [D3-04-F13] |
19	| Ludhiana, urban health centre | 40 with diabetes | "side effects of taking medications daily"; "about 50% patients were adherent" [D3-04-F14] |
20	| Chennai and Chunampet | 54 (patients, caregivers, providers, officials) | Caregivers enable access for older adults; "shared device ownership"; "data privacy, security, and app reliability affected trust" [D3-04-F05] |
21	
22	Karnataka patients suggested reminders and digital records [D3-04-F01]. A FORUM POST by an adult child says the father's pressure stayed controlled on Ayurvedic treatment, then rose, and he "re-started some medication" [D3-04-F52].
23	
24	So what for us (OUR VIEW): feeling well recurs as a reason to stop, and a home reading is one thing that can contradict it.
25	
26	### Home monitors in Indian homes
27	
28	Few patients own a home cuff, most taught themselves, and home readings show that many "controlled" patients are not.
29	
30	- **Who has one.** Of 2,588 clinic-attending people with hypertension and caregivers in North India, 18.1% used a home monitor (urban 20.5%, rural 8.5%) [D3-04-F06]. No household figure exists; a web claim of under 5% cites no source [D3-04-F22].
31	- **Who taught them.** 75.2% reported "learning HBPM themselves through observation, videos, and reading"; 24.7% were trained by a health worker. Technique was excellent in 15.9% of patients and 5.9% of caregivers [D3-04-F06].
32	- **Do doctors act on home readings.** About 88% of 832 Indian doctors recommend home monitoring, but estimate only 30.4% of patients measure; 31.3% say to measure before tablets, about 30% give no instructions [D3-04-F07]. Only 15.1% knew the correct home thresholds [D3-04-F18].
33	- **What home readings reveal.** In GRAND (18 centres, 12 states, 1,920 treated regular attenders, 7 days of home readings), 77.7% looked controlled by clinic pressure but 55.9% by clinic plus home; 21.8% had masked uncontrolled pressure (high at home, normal in clinic) [D3-04-F09]. Median knowledge of home monitoring was 1 out of 7 [D3-04-F10].
34	
35	So what for us (OUR VIEW): the loop must bring the cuff, the teaching and the thresholds.
36	
37	### What doctors and health workers say
38	
39	Doctors describe heavy workloads, and many private doctors do not follow the state protocol.
40	
41	- **Workload.** In Kolar, Karnataka: "Doctors face very high workloads, especially in the public sector"; care is "very doctor-centred" [D3-04-F16]. Meghalaya reports staff vacancies and limited training [D3-04-F12, D3-04-F20].
42	- **The state protocol.** Of 30 private doctors in Bhopal, 19 did not follow it, citing "fear of either losing patients due to a lack of immediate blood pressure control or causing drug-related adverse effects" and a preference for fixed-dose combinations (two drugs in one tablet) [D3-04-F15].
43	- **Health workers with a decision tool.** IMPACT Diabetes, a cluster trial in 16 villages in two states (418 people, 9 months): ASHAs (village health workers) with a tablet tool under physician supervision, against usual care. HbA1c (average blood sugar over about three months) fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3%; physician visits 85.0% against 29.8%; "acceptable and feasible for patients, ASHAs, and physicians" [D3-04-F17]. Diabetes, not blood pressure.
44	
45	Not found: any Indian doctor, nurse or health worker on dose steps from home readings, or any qualitative study of ASHAs on blood-pressure follow-up.
46	
47	So what for us (OUR VIEW): a doctor's approval cannot be assumed.
48

50	
51	The latest 100 Apple App Store India reviews each of three diabetes programmes, BeatO, Sugar.fit and Fitterfly, were read on 13 Nov 2026. One-star reviews: 55, 76 and 9 (count from the research note's method section); Fitterfly's 5-star profile looks prompted (the note's inference). All quotes are PUBLIC REVIEW, verbatim.

(Fitterfly, 23 Apr 2025) [D3-04-F43] | "Now my HBA1c reduced to 6.1 and medicine also reduced to half." (Fitterfly, 10 Nov 2024) [D3-04-F44] |

62	None of the 300 reviews mentions language or voice, and none describes a dose change from a home reading (count from the research note's method section).
63	
64	### Reminders and messages
65	
66	In a Punjab trial at two public hospitals, 388 patients with uncontrolled pressure got two myth-busting WhatsApp reminders before their visit or none; attendance was 21.8% against 19.6%, a null result, and beliefs did not change [D3-04-F50]. A Delhi study of 110 patients (counselling, voice calls, SMS) reported control rising from 14.7% to 52.9%, with no control group [D3-04-F51].
67	The phone is often not the patient's. Caregivers enable access and devices are shared [D3-04-F05]; one review moves a meter from a husband's phone to a mother's [D3-04-F25]. 54% of women aged 15-49 own the phone they use, 46.6% in rural areas [D3-04-F23]. Among 150 rural older adults near Mysore, 50% owned a phone, few a smartphone, and digital literacy was 11% [D3-04-F56]. About 10.6% of Indians spoke English in 2011 [D3-04-F57].
68	
69	So what for us (OUR VIEW): a message only works if it reaches the person who holds the phone and leads to a decision.
70	
71	### Two field voices from people who run programmes
72	
73	Both are LinkedIn posts, paraphrased; numbers inside them are unverified.
74	
75	- A national NCD (non-communicable disease) consultant at UNICEF India, about Apr 2026: programmes failed on BP machines uncalibrated for months and mid-month drug stock-outs; one protocol, steady supply and the Simple app made missed visits visible. Claims control rose 48 percentage points in primary care and 23 in secondary (POST CLAIM, source not named) (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).
76	- A doctor and WHO consultant, about Oct 2026: counting visits is not enough; programmes must know who continues, who is controlled and who missed follow-up. Cites mWellcare: a digital system does not guarantee results (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).
77	
78	Neither describes dose changes from home readings.
79	
80	### What we could not find
81	
82	A household figure for cuff ownership; any Indian clinician voice on dose steps from home readings; any patient voice on a dose increase; voice against text preference among older patients; Reddit posts (the archive timed out) and Google Play reviews.
83	
84	### So what for us
85	
86	OUR VIEW:
87	- **Assume most patients do not own a cuff.** Supply one and teach the technique; only 18.1% used one even among clinic attenders [D3-04-F06].
88	- **A doctor may not trust the state protocol.** Each proposal must show why the step is safe, answering the fears of slow control and side effects [D3-04-F15].
89	- **Never rely on a reminder alone.** WhatsApp reminders did not raise attendance [D3-04-F50]; the reading must lead to a decision.
90	- **Design for the household phone.** Reach whoever holds it, by voice, in the local language [D3-04-F05, D3-04-F23].
91	- **Risk: home readings bring bad news.** 21.8% of treated clinic attenders had masked uncontrolled pressure [D3-04-F09]; expect fear of more drugs and the urge to stop [D3-04-F02].

3	### What this part shows
4	
5	Across six disease areas, a home reading improved outcomes when it led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when it was only displayed or turned into a reminder. This part sets out the trials behind that pattern, their safety record, the Indian results (including one important null result), and what a doctor would need before trusting a product built on them.
6

12	
13	Each row sets a result where the reading changed the treatment beside one where it was only shown or used for a reminder. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.

16	|---|---|---|

Patient self-titration: -9.2 mmHg at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. Pharmacists adjusting drugs: 57.2% against 30.0% controlled [D1-01-F04]. | Self-monitoring alone: -1.0 mmHg (95% CI -3.3 to 1.2), no effect [D1-01-F05]. Reminder app: -0.5 mmHg, p=0.78 [D1-01-F06]. |

Structured remote management: all-cause death HR 0.70 [D1-01-F30]. | Daily symptoms and weight sent to own clinicians: 52.3% against 51.5% readmission or death [D1-01-F32]. Telemonitoring reviewed by central nurses with protocol actions and calls, but no mandated dose protocol: aHR 1.03 [D1-01-F33]. Pooled passive telemonitoring: death RR 0.93, not significant [D1-01-F54]. |

21	| Asthma | Patient raises the steroid dose with each reliever puff (SMART): exacerbations RR 0.68 [D1-02-F37]. | Inhaler reminders: adherence 84% against 30%, school absence 1.9% against 1.7% of days, no difference [D1-02-F01]. Sensor inhaler system: odds ratio for control 1.35, credible interval 0.846 to 2.038, crossing 1 [D1-02-F02]. |
22	| Tuberculosis adherence | No trial in the notes changed the treatment from adherence data. In China the planned step (doctor moves non-adherent patients to intensive management) was "underutilised" [D1-02-F34]. | Smart pillboxes or labels, four countries, 23,483 patients: poor outcomes not reduced (adjusted ratios 1.13 to 1.49, all intervals crossing 1) [D1-02-F59]. |
23	
24	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the active ingredient is the treatment change, not the sensor and not the nudge. A product that stops at showing a reading sits in the right-hand column, where results are mostly null.

27

32	Blood pressure has the deepest evidence: primary-care titration trials, a 33,995-person trial of dose stepping by village health workers with four-year hard outcomes, and South Asian and Indian trials, including a null result that shows where a product should not try to add value.

34	#### (a) Trials where home readings led to a medicine change

37	|---|---|---|---|---|---|

40	| TASMINH4, 2018 | UK, 142 practices | 1,182 | GP titrated from home readings, sent on paper or by telemonitoring | Usual care using clinic readings | Clinic systolic -3.5 mmHg (paper) and -4.7 (telemonitoring) at 12 months [D1-01-F03] |
