A pooled analysis of individual patient data from 15 trials (7,138 people) found self-monitoring worked best in people on fewer drugs and with baseline systolic up to 170 [D1-01-F05].
44	
45	#### (b) Dose stepping by non-physicians at scale
46	
47	The China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP) was an open cluster trial in 326 villages with 33,995 people aged 40 and over [D1-01-F09]. Village doctors (community health workers) started and stepped drugs by a standard protocol, supervised by primary-care physicians, and coached patients on home BP monitoring. The comparator was enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09].
48	
49	- **18 months:** BP under 130/80 in 57.0% against 19.9%, a difference of 37.0 points (95% CI 34.9 to 39.1); systolic 14.5 mmHg lower, diastolic 7.1 lower; no treatment-related serious adverse events [D1-01-F09].
50	- **4 years (median), age 60 and over (22,386 people):** cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, heart-failure admission, cardiovascular death) 2.7% against 3.5% a year, HR 0.75 (0.69 to 0.81); all-cause death HR 0.90 (0.83 to 0.98) [D1-01-F38].
51	- **4 years, under 60 (11,609 people):** cardiovascular events HR 0.64 (0.56 to 0.75); stroke 0.64; heart failure 0.39; cardiovascular death 0.54 [D1-01-F38].
52	- **Safety at 4 years:** injurious falls, symptomatic low BP, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups in either age band [D1-01-F38].
53	
54	The caveat. The trial registry entry (opened by the claims check) says the intervention also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates [D1-01-F38]. The effect therefore cannot be credited to the protocol alone.
55	
56	#### (c) The Indian evidence
57	
58	**The national programme's surveys.** The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) surveyed the same 9 districts in 5 states twice. In 2018-19, of 7,047 people with hypertension, 52.4% were aware, 40.8% treated and 14.5% controlled; in two districts control was under 5% [D1-01-F10]. In 2023-24, of 7,324, 58.5% were aware, 44.7% treated and 21.2% controlled, a gain of 6.7 points in control [D1-01-F11]. This is a before-after survey with no control districts [D1-01-F11]. In the IHCI cohort of 21,895 registered patients, 51% returned for follow-up; among those who returned, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
59	
60	**The South Asian trial.** COBRA-BPS was a cluster trial in 30 rural communities in Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka with 2,645 adults with hypertension, run for 24 months [D1-01-F37]. Government community health workers made home visits for BP monitoring and counselling; physicians were trained; care was coordinated in the public sector. Systolic fell 9.0 against 3.9 mmHg, a difference of 5.2 (3.2 to 7.1); control under 140/90 was 53.2% against 43.7%, RR 1.22; all-cause death 2.9% against 4.3%, with no confidence interval in the abstract [D1-01-F37]. Health workers monitored and referred; trained physicians changed the drugs [D1-01-F37]. Post-hoc, patients got about 0.11 more drugs each [D1-01-F12].
61	
62	**The decision-support trial that found nothing.** mWellcare was an open cluster trial in 40 community health centres in India with 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, run for 12 months [D1-01-F46]. Nurse-managed care with an Android app giving algorithm-based management prompts, a health record and reminders was compared with enhanced usual care. Systolic difference -0.98 mmHg (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67); HbA1c +0.11 (-0.24 to 0.45). Both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. The authors: "We did not find an incremental benefit of mWellcare over enhanced usual care" [D1-01-F46].
63	
64	OUR VIEW, what the null result means:
65	- Prompting a nurse or doctor during a clinic visit added nothing over a well-run protocol programme that already produced a 13 mmHg fall [D1-01-F46].
66	- The app worked at the visit. It did not act on home readings between visits, and it did not reach patients who never came back.
67	
68	OUR VIEW, what it does not mean:
69	- It does not show that between-visit titration fails in India. The notes found no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a titration protocol (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
70	- It does not show that protocols fail. The enhanced usual-care arm improved as much as the app arm.
71	
72	Contrast a South Asian diabetes trial, CARRS: non-physician care coordinators plus physician decision-support software doubled the chance of improving HbA1c, BP and LDL cholesterol together, RR 2.1 (1.5 to 2.8) at 12 months [D1-01-F23]. OUR VIEW: the extra ingredient was a person following patients up.
73	
74	A secondary analysis of a company-linked Indian diabetes trial (Twin Health) used home BP to guide drug changes: systolic -7.6 against -3.2 mmHg, in small subgroups [D1-01-F20].
75	
76	#### (d) A lifestyle-only prescription app in Japan
77	
78	HERB-DH1 tested CureApp HT, an app giving personalised lifestyle coaching with no drug change (adaptive depth 3), in 390 untreated adults with hypertension at 12 sites in Japan, open-label, for 12 weeks [D1-01-F07]. Against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour ambulatory systolic -2.4 mmHg (95% CI -4.5 to -0.3), home -4.3, office -3.6; no major programme-related safety events to 24 weeks [D1-01-F07]. CureApp HT was approved in April 2022 and covered by national health insurance from 1 September 2022, prescribed by doctors (THEIR CLAIM for "first worldwide") [D1-01-F57]. A price of about 8,000 yen, with the patient paying 30%, appears in a search summary only [D1-01-F57]; the company's June 2026 release gives 7,010 yen for the app as an insured material (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-04-F43].
79	
80	OUR VIEW: it moved BP about half as much as the titration trials, in patients not yet on drugs; depth 3 helps a little but does not replace dose changes.
81	
82	#### (e) What telemonitoring adds once someone is titrating
83	
84	Little. In TASMINH4, telemonitoring against paper self-monitoring, with the GP titrating in both arms, gave -1.2 mmHg (95% CI -3.5 to 1.2), not significant [D1-01-F03]. The independent US review by PHTI (Peterson Health Technology Institute, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful", and said monitoring "may support adoption for providers who consistently act on monitoring data" [D1-01-F39]. It rated medication-management programmes, where virtual care teams adjust drugs, "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg systolic fall [D1-01-F39].
85	
86	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the authority to change the dose between visits, and someone acting on it, is what worked. Electronics added little once a clinician was titrating. Our product's value must sit where mWellcare did not look: between visits, from home readings, among the half who do not return.
87	
88	### Diabetes
89	
90	In type 2 diabetes the same split holds: software that changes the insulin dose works, and monitoring or coaching alone gives small gains. Closed-loop insulin, where the device changes the dose itself every few minutes, is the model case of an adaptive therapy.
91	
92	**Insulin-dose software (adaptive depth 4).**
93	- d-Nav, 2019: randomised trial, 181 adults on insulin with HbA1c 7.5-11%, 3 US centres, 6 months. A handheld device measured glucose and computed the next dose, plus clinician support, against clinician support alone (both arms 7 contacts). HbA1c fell 1.0% against 0.3% (p<0.0001); low blood sugar 0.29 against 0.29 events a month. Funded by the US NIH [D1-01-F13].
94	- TeleDiab-2, 2019: randomised, 191 adults starting basal (long-acting) insulin, 4 months. A phone voice system and an app both proposed daily dose changes towards a fasting glucose of about 100 mg/dL. HbA1c -1.44% and -1.48% against -0.92%. No severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The country (France) comes from the research agent's knowledge, not the abstract [D1-01-F14].
95	- Sanofi My Dose Coach has observational data only: in the US, 2,517 users, 44% reached their fasting target, low blood sugar in 12-16% of users [D1-01-F15]; in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, 494 users, 55.9% reached target in a mean 14.8 days, low blood sugar 1.4% [D1-01-F16]. Neither had a control group. Its status in India is unknown (search summary only) [D1-04-F09].
96	
97	**Glucose sensors with and without an algorithm.**
98	- Sensor alone (CGM, continuous glucose monitor), not on insulin: IMMEDIATE, 116 adults, 16 weeks, time in range up 9.9 points, HbA1c 0.3% lower (95% CI 0 to 0.7) [D1-01-F17].
99	- Sensor alone, on basal insulin: MOBILE, 175 adults, 15 US centres, 8 months: HbA1c 0.4% lower (-0.8 to -0.1). Funded by Dexcom, the sensor maker [D1-01-F42].
100	- Sensor plus algorithm: 2IQP, 2025, 319 adults on insulin, US and Canada, 13 weeks. Automated insulin delivery against own insulin method, with a sensor in both arms. HbA1c 0.6 points lower (-0.8 to -0.4); time in range 14 points higher. Funded by Tandem, the pump maker [D1-01-F43]. Because both arms had a sensor, this isolates what the dose-changing algorithm adds.
101	
102	**Closed loop as the model case.** In type 1 diabetes, Control-IQ (168 people, 6 months) raised time in range by 11 points against a sensor-augmented pump and ran in closed-loop mode 90% of the time [D1-01-F24]. The iLet bionic pancreas (326 people, 13 weeks) started from body weight alone with no carbohydrate counting and lowered HbA1c by 0.5 [D1-01-F25]. In type 2 diabetes, a 26-person crossover trial with no meal doses gave time in range 66.3% against 32.3% [D1-01-F26]. A 2026 review says the American Diabetes Association now supports automated delivery as the preferred method for some type 2 patients; the ADA text itself was not opened [D1-01-F45].
103	
104	**Nutrition and "digital twin" results, with caveats.**
105	- Zeevi 2015, Israel, 800 people: a model predicted each person's post-meal glucose; HbA1c was not the outcome [D1-01-F22]. ZOE METHOD (347 US adults, mostly without diabetes, company-sponsored): triglycerides -0.13 mmol/L [D1-01-F55].
106	- Twin Health, India, 319 people, open-label, 2:1: HbA1c -2.9 against -0.3 at 1 year and "72.7% remission"; the remission definition and drug-withdrawal rules are not in the abstract, and author company links were not checked [D1-01-F19].
107	- Twin Health, Cleveland Clinic, 150 people, single site: HbA1c 6.5% or under on no drug except metformin, 71% against 2.4%. Read through a trade article only [D1-01-F56].
108	- Virta: not randomised (262 against 87, self-selected). At 2 years, use of diabetes drugs other than metformin fell from 55.7% to 26.8% [D1-01-F21].
109	
110	**The independent verdict.** PHTI (March 2024) found US digital tools for type 2 diabetes without a continuous glucose monitor "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits and result in a higher cost than usual care", with gains "minimal and short-term" [D1-01-F40]. The two exceptions were people with higher HbA1c newly starting insulin, and nutritional ketosis programmes [D1-01-F40]. PHTI's new review of sensor and GLP-1 support reports in 2027 [D1-01-F41].
111	
112	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: insulin titration is the second protocol for the same loop and has trial support, but low blood sugar makes it riskier, and the large nutrition effects come from company-linked or non-randomised studies.
113	
114	### Heart failure
115	
116	Heart failure gives the sharpest contrast in the notes: fast dose stepping cut death or readmission by a third, while several large telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol were null.
117	
118	**Fast dose stepping.** STRONG-HF (2022) was an open-label trial in 87 hospitals in 14 countries with 1,078 patients admitted with acute heart failure [D1-01-F27]. The high-intensity arm raised drugs to full recommended doses within 2 weeks of discharge, with 4 visits in 2 months checking symptoms, lab tests and NT-proBNP (a blood marker of heart strain). At day 90, full doses: RAS blockers 55% against 2%, beta blockers 49% against 4%. Readmission or death at 180 days: 15.2% against 23.3% (adjusted estimates, not raw shares), RR 0.66 (0.50 to 0.86); the high-intensity arm also reported more side effects (see Safety). The trial stopped early for benefit. Funder: Roche Diagnostics, maker of NT-proBNP tests [D1-01-F27]. Benefit by age: HR 0.51 under 65, 0.73 over 65, no significant difference [D1-01-F28]. A Russian chatbot titration trial (66 patients, 6 weeks) saw 2 against 16 decompensations or deaths but lost 7 of 33 remote patients [D1-01-F51].
119	
120	**Telemonitoring: positive and negative trials.**
121	
122	| Trial | Patients, place | What happened to the reading | Result |
123	|---|---|---|---|
124	| TELE-HF, 2010 | 1,653, USA | Daily symptoms and weight by phone, reviewed by patients' own clinicians | Readmission or death 52.3% against 51.5%, null [D1-01-F32] |
125	| BEAT-HF, 2016 | 1,437, California | BP, pulse, weight reviewed by central nurses with protocol actions and phone calls; no mandated dose protocol | Readmission aHR 1.03, null; better quality of life [D1-01-F33] |
126	| GUIDE-HF, 2021 | 1,000, US and Canada | Implanted lung-artery pressure sensor guiding care | HR 0.88 (0.74 to 1.05), neutral overall [D1-01-F34] |
127	| TIM-HF2, 2018 | 1,571, Germany | Structured remote management | Days lost ratio 0.80 (p=0.046); death HR 0.70 (0.50 to 0.96) [D1-01-F30] |
128	
129	OUR VIEW on what separates them: the positive trials had a structured team or explicit dose targets; the null ones sent data to clinicians or nurses without a mandated dose protocol (BEAT-HF's nurses did follow protocol actions). TIM-HF2's benefit grew with distance to a cardiologist, 13% lower risk per doubling of distance [D1-01-F31]. The TELE-HF authors stressed "a thorough, independent evaluation of disease-management strategies before their adoption" [D1-01-F32].
130	
131	**Pooled analyses, which conflict.** A 2026 meta-analysis of 79 trials (31,669 patients) found remote monitoring cut heart-failure admissions (IRR 0.81) and death (RR 0.90) with no difference by method [D1-01-F53]. Another 2026 meta-analysis of 16 trials (8,618) found a gradient: pressure-guided RR 0.71, structured remote management 0.79, non-invasive telemonitoring alone 0.93, not significant; the authors wrote "passive telemonitoring alone is insufficient" [D1-01-F54]. They used different trial sets [D1-01-F54].
132	
133	**The Indian treatment gap.** In the Trivandrum registry (1,205 admissions, 16 hospitals, Kerala, 2013), only 25% of patients with weak pumping were discharged on all three drug classes, and 5-year mortality was 59% [D1-01-F35]. The national registry (10,851 patients, 53 hospitals) found 47.5% of eligible patients on guideline drugs, 90-day mortality 14.2% [D1-01-F47] and 1-year 22.1% [D1-01-F48]. A second registry (5,182 patients) found adherence to all three classes of 18.8% in men and 15.9% in women; one registry counts prescriptions, the other adherence [D1-01-F49]. After a heart attack with weak pumping, use of one class (MRA) fell from 69% to 6% within a year [D1-01-F50]. The registries report drug classes, not dose levels [D1-01-F35, D1-01-F47].
134	
135	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: heart failure fits the challenge's "far from a specialist" best, but the working loop needs lab values and visits, so it belongs on the roadmap, not in tonight's build.
136	
137	### Other conditions, briefly
138	
139	The other conditions repeat the pattern and add two lessons: a dose loop can work with no sensor at all, and rehabilitation by software matches in-person care without beating usual care.
140	
141	- **Warfarin.** A Cochrane review of 28 trials (8,950 patients) found that patients who tested INR at home and adjusted their own dose by a schedule had fewer clots (RR 0.47) and lower death (RR 0.55). Patients who tested at home and left the dose to the clinic had fewer clots (RR 0.69) but no change in death (RR 0.94). Each approach was compared with usual care in separate sets of trials, not with each other. Major bleeding did not change overall (RR 0.95) [D1-02-F05].
142	- **Gout.** In a UK trial (517 patients, Nottingham, 2 years), nurses titrating urate-lowering drugs to a target reached it in 95% against 30% under GP care, RR 3.18, at £5,066 per quality-adjusted life year. It was not digital: it was a protocol run by nurses [D1-02-F06].
143	- **Asthma and COPD.** SMART (one inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose) cut exacerbations by RR 0.68 in 16 trials with 22,748 people aged 12 and over [D1-02-F37]. No sensor was needed because the patient's own reliever use is the signal and the inhaler delivers the dose change at that moment. Sensor inhalers did less: reminders raised adherence without changing school absence [D1-02-F01]; the Digihaler system's benefit interval crossed 1 and adherence fell from 79.2% to 68.6% over 6 months [D1-02-F02]; a Propeller trial cut reliever use but not asthma control scores overall (company-affiliated authors) [D1-02-F38]. Commercially, Teva withdrew the Digihaler app and US inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41], and an undated ResMed page says Propeller "has ceased operations" [D1-02-F40].
144	- **Rehabilitation by software.** Stroke telerehab after discharge was no better than usual care for daily-living activities (SMD 0.00) and about equal to in-person physiotherapy [D1-02-F07]. Lung telerehab, 99% COPD, matched centre rehab on walking distance, with completion 93% against 70% [D1-02-F03]. A Sword Health trial (140 back-pain patients, company-affiliated) found no difference in disability against in-person physiotherapy but lower dropout, 15.7% against 34.3% [D1-02-F08]. PHTI (June 2024) found physiotherapist-guided virtual care comparable to in-person care with lower spending, app-only exercise "unlikely to be effective as total substitutes", and did not separate the effect of adapting exercise to measured performance [D1-02-F54].
145	- **Biofeedback and stimulation.** Device-guided breathing lowered systolic BP by 3.67 mmHg across 8 trials, but showed no effect once the 5 manufacturer-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11]. Nerivio, a sham-controlled migraine stimulator, gave pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% against 38.8%, but it uses no sensor loop [D1-02-F12].
146	
147	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: a sensor earns its place only if it changes a decision that a cheaper signal cannot. Warfarin and SMART show the dose rule itself carries the benefit.

168	### Drop-off and adherence technology
169	
170	People stop using health apps quickly, and the trials show that raising adherence on its own often leaves outcomes unchanged.
171	
172	**Retention.**
173	- 93 Android mental-health apps with 10,000 or more installs (2019): the median app kept 3.3% of users at day 30 [D1-02-F26].
174	- Eight remote US studies, over 100,000 people: median retention 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27].
175	- Chronic-disease app trials: pooled dropout 43% (40% in randomised trials, 49% in observational studies) [D1-02-F28].
176	- Engagement strategies helped modestly, SMD 0.33, very low certainty [D1-02-F56].
177	- With a clinician in the loop, retention was higher: Sword dropout 15.7% [D1-02-F08]; lung telerehab completion 93% [D1-02-F03].
178	
179	**Adherence rose; outcomes did not.**
180

182	|---|---|---|---|
183	| Inhaler reminders, New Zealand, 2015 | 220 children, 6 months | 84% against 30% | School absence 1.9% against 1.7%, no difference [D1-02-F01] |

204	| Insulin | My Dose Coach, no control | Low blood sugar in 12-16% of US users [D1-01-F15], 1.4% in the Gulf [D1-01-F16] |
205	| Closed loop | Control-IQ; iLet | Time below 70 mg/dL fell; 1 diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA, a dangerous acid build-up) [D1-01-F24]. Severe low blood sugar 17.7 against 10.8 per 100 patient-years, not significant [D1-01-F25] |
206	| Closed loop, type 2 | CamAPS HX; 2IQP; twiist | 1 serious adverse event [D1-01-F26]; 1 severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F43]; 1 DKA, no control arm [D1-01-F44] |
207	| Heart failure | STRONG-HF | Any adverse event by day 90: 41% against 29%; serious 16% against 17%; fatal 5% against 6% [D1-01-F27]; similar by age [D1-01-F28] |
208	| Heart failure | Chatbot titration, Russia | Potassium and kidney function no different at 6 weeks [D1-01-F51] |
209	
210	Not in the notes: potassium and kidney event rates by arm in STRONG-HF (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
211	
212	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: protocol titration has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. The known costs are more minor side effects, leg swelling in self-managed BP care, and low blood sugar with insulin, so each needs its own safety branch.
213	
214	### What a doctor in a small town would ask
215	
216	OUR VIEW. These are the questions we expect, with what the evidence can and cannot answer.
217	
218	1. **Time saved.** A primary-care consultation in India lasted about 2 minutes in 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24], and 79.9% of required posts in four specialities (surgeon, physician, obstetrician-gynaecologist, paediatrician) in rural community health centres were unfilled in March 2023 [D1-03-F16]. A product that adds screens to the visit repeats mWellcare [D1-01-F46]. It must do the reading, the protocol logic and the draft, and leave one approve-or-change action. How long approval takes in practice: NOT RESEARCHED.
219	2. **Which protocol.** Doctors will trust a protocol they already use. Trials that worked used pre-agreed plans or standard protocols [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F09]; an Indian state protocol with steps, thresholds and 30-day re-checks already exists [D1-06-F14].
220	3. **Can I overrule it.** In every positive BP trial a named person held the authority: patient by a pre-agreed plan, GP, pharmacist or supervised village doctor [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09]. The design must let the doctor change or refuse any proposal, and record why.
221	4. **Are home readings valid.** Home and clinic targets differ (TASMIN-SR used a home target of 120/75) [D1-01-F02]; reading rules are in part E.
222	5. **Who is liable** if a proposed step harms a patient, and what licence the tool needs. The notes in this part cannot answer this; see part F2.
223	6. **Who pays me** for the time. Not answerable here; see part F2.
224	
225	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: a doctor will judge the product on minutes and liability before outcomes.
226	
227	### What we could not find
228	
229	- An Indian randomised trial of home BP readings driving a titration protocol (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
230	- Potassium and kidney rates by arm in STRONG-HF; GOALS-HF results [D1-01-F52].
231	- PHTI's category-level mmHg figures for hypertension (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
232	- Dose levels in any Indian heart-failure registry [D1-01-F35].
233	- Rejoyn's primary publication and sales [D1-02-F49].
234	- Indian evidence for warfarin, gout, asthma or rehab loops (D1-02, NOT SEARCHED list).
235	- Only the facts the claims checks (D3-01, D3-02) reached have been re-verified; their corrections are applied here.
236	
237	### So what for us
238	
239	OUR VIEW.
240	- Build at adaptive depth 4: the reading must come back as a proposed dose change, or we sit with the null trials [D1-01-F05, D1-01-F39].
241	- Give the decision to a named person under a written protocol, and make approving it take seconds; electronics added little once someone titrated [D1-01-F03, D1-01-F09].
242	- Aim at the gap mWellcare left: between visits and among the 49% who do not return [D1-01-F46, D1-03-F10].
243	- Treat adherence as an input to the dose rule, never as the product [D1-02-F59, D1-01-F06].
244	- Write a safety branch for each known harm (swelling, low BP, falls, kidney, low sugar) and report it from day one [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F38].

1	## D2. How care has been scaled without specialists
2	
3	### What this part shows
4	
5	India and other low-income settings have raised blood-pressure control without specialists by giving routine work to nurses and health workers under a written protocol, backed by free drugs and regular refills. In India the dose change still waits for a doctor's visit, and that is where a home step loop could fit.
6	
7	### India's hypertension programme in practice
8	
9	The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) shows what a protocol programme does well, and where patients drop out.
10	
11	**Design choices**
12	- A protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first. Punjab: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg (to 80 mg), then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (to 25 mg). Maharashtra orders the steps differently [D3-05-F01].
13	- Free drugs, given as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres (HWC) to district hospitals; sub-centres are not named [D3-05-F02].
14	- The open-source Simple app: about 80 seconds to register a patient, 15 seconds for a follow-up, overdue lists with high-risk patients first, one-click nurse calls, automated reminders [D3-05-F03].
15	
16	**Who does what.** Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up; Senior Treatment Supervisors support training. Who steps the dose in Maharashtra is not stated [D3-05-F06].
17	
18	**Starts and losses.** Two cohorts give different loss figures; they differ in sites, years and definition:
19	
20	| Cohort | Started | Not seen again | Control among those seen |
21	|---|---|---|---|
22	| 24 sentinel sites, 4 states, registered 2018-19 | 21,895 | 49% (51% returned by Jul-Sep 2019) | 26.3% at registration, 59.8% at follow-up [D1-03-F10] |
23	| Punjab and Maharashtra, started 2018-2021 | 281,209 | 36% (no visit Jan-Mar 2022) | 70% and 76% on amlodipine 5 mg alone; 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04] |
24	
25	District surveys found 14.5% of people with hypertension controlled in 2018-19 and 21.2% in 2023-24, with no control districts [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11]. The programme's own deck claims 75 million people with hypertension and/or diabetes on standard care by December 2025 (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F10].
26	
27	**Why patients stopped.** A Bathinda (Punjab) phone survey of 157 people who had missed visits for over 3 months, a small convenience sample: no sense of being ill 24.8%, distance 22.2%, no guidance or reminder 15.2%, acute illness 8.2% [D3-05-F07].
28	
29	**The refill rule.** A doctor dispenses the first medicine. Trained paramedical staff dispense the monthly refill only when pressure is controlled; uncontrolled patients are sent to a doctor for a dose change [D3-05-F08].
30	
31	**Cost.** Amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year [D3-05-F05]. A 2022 WHO release gives "as low as Rs 200" per patient per year, a modelled drug cost (SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D3-05-F09]. Neither includes staff; a full cost was not found.
32	
33	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor.
34	
35	### Who may change a dose in India
36	
37	- Opened source: in Bathinda, paramedical staff refill only when pressure is controlled; uncontrolled patients go to a doctor [D3-05-F08].
38	- Search summary only: state protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose; once controlled, the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) at the HWC or sub-centre measures pressure and gives a month's medicines [D3-05-F31].
39	- Search summary only: community health officer (CHO) duties are screening, referral and follow-up; starting treatment sits with the medical officer and staff nurse [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13].
40	- NOT FOUND: any order letting a CHO or nurse start or change an antihypertensive dose. The 2023-2030 national NCD guidelines could not be opened.
41	
42	We cannot say they may, nor that they are barred. It remains a question for state health departments and a lawyer.
43	
44	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.
45	
46	### Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme
47	
48	Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam (MTM) brings screening and medicines to the home [D3-05-F15].
49	- Scale: launched August 2021; by August 2024, 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14].
50	- Women health volunteers deliver drugs to registered patients over 45 or with poor mobility (search summary only) [D3-05-F16].
51	- A 2025 survey of 6,856 adults: over 95% of those diagnosed on treatment, but a hypertension control rate of only 35.4% (the abstract does not state the denominator) [D1-03-F09].
52	- **It refills; it does not step.** No source says the dose is changed at the door; delivery continues the existing prescription [D3-05-F15].
53	
54	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the drugs already reach the door at the same dose; high treatment with low control is the gap a dose step addresses.
55	
56	### Programmes outside India
57	
58	| Programme, size | Who decides the dose | Who delivers | Also in the package | Result | Comparison group |
59	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
60	| China rural project; 326 villages, 33,995 | Village doctors by protocol, physician-supervised | Village doctors | Free or discounted drugs; doctors paid on control rate; audit; free home cuffs (search summary only) | Under 130/80 at 18 months 57.0% vs 19.9%; 4-year events HR 0.75 (60+), 0.64 (under 60); no rise in falls | Yes, cluster trial [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38, D3-05-F21] |
61	| Lesotho; 103 villages, 547 | Lay village health workers, by app | Same workers | One fixed-dose pill | Under 140/90 at 12 months 58% vs 48%, p=0.046 | Yes, cluster trial vs facility referral [D3-05-F24] |
62	| IMPACT-BP, South Africa; 774 | Nurses remotely by app (not stated explicitly) | Health worker at home collects readings, delivers medicine | Home cuff | Systolic 7.9-9.1 mmHg lower at 6 months; control 57.6% vs 76.9-82.8% (ACC summary) or about 32% vs 60% (GroundUp, time point not stated) | Yes, vs standard care [D3-05-F27] |
63	| Nigeria; 60 centres, 21,922 | Health workers under standing orders (search summary only) | Centre staff | Free drugs, then US$1.60 co-pay a month; single pills 16.3% to 65.2%; 30-day stock 27% to 96% of centres | Control 21.7% to 55.9% (2020-2023) | No [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F23] |
64	| Uganda HIV clinic; 1,082 | Clinic | Clinic | 3-month refills once controlled | Control 73.5% to 78.3%; 96.4% retained | No [D3-05-F36] |
65	| COBRA-BPS, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka; 2,645 | Trained physicians; health workers did not change doses | Health worker home visits | Counselling, coordination | Systolic 5.2 mmHg lower at 24 months | Yes, cluster trial [D1-01-F37] |
66	| CARRS, India and Pakistan; 1,146 | Physicians, with software prompts | Care coordinators calling monthly | Low-cost generics | Combined target 18.2% vs 8.7%; more mild lows | Yes, 28 months [D3-05-F18] |
67	| mWellcare, India; 3,698 | Nurse-managed care, app prompts | Nurses | Reminders | Systolic difference 0.98 mmHg (CI -4.64 to 2.67): null | Yes, 12 months [D1-01-F46] |
68	| Kaiser, US (search summary only) | Not stated | Medical assistants | Registry, single pill | Control 43.6% (2001) to 80.4% (2009) | No [D3-05-F20] |
69	| PAHO HEARTS, 33 countries | Roadmap names nurse dose adjustment | Primary care | Multi-month prescriptions | About 60% where fully run (THEIR CLAIM) | No [D3-05-F28] |
70	
71	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the largest controlled gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing.
72	
73	### What the fixes are worth
74	
75	| Fix | Evidence |
76	|---|---|
77	| Longer refills | Uganda 3-month refills: 96.4% retained, control 73.5% to 78.3%, no control group [D3-05-F36] |
78	| Single-pill combinations | Systolic 3.99 mmHg lower at week 12 vs separate pills; mostly observational (search summary only) [D3-05-F39] |
79	| Home delivery | IMPACT-BP home arm 7.9 mmHg lower [D3-05-F27] |
80	| Phone follow-up | Calls beat generic reminders, "moderately effective" (search summary only) [D3-05-F41]; no Indian trial isolates calls |
81	
82	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: each fix keeps patients on drugs; none changes the dose.
83	
84	### What these programmes changed that software alone could not
85	
86	- Drug stock: Nigeria [D3-05-F22]; IHCI [D3-05-F02]; China [D1-01-F38].
87	- Authority for a non-doctor to change drugs: China [D1-01-F09]; Lesotho [D3-05-F24]; PAHO roadmap [D3-05-F28].
88	- A person carrying medicine to the home: IMPACT-BP [D3-05-F27]; Tamil Nadu [D3-05-F14].
89	- Pay linked to control and physician audit: China [D3-05-F21].
90	- A person who phones and books visits: CARRS [D3-05-F18]; IHCI nurses [D3-05-F03].
91	- Software alone, mWellcare, added nothing [D1-01-F46].
92	
93	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.
94	
95	### Where a home step loop fits (OUR VIEW)
96	
97	**What it adds to IHCI today**
98	- The dose step for patients who do not return (36-49% [D3-05-F04, D1-03-F10]), who now need a doctor's visit to step up [D3-05-F08]. The loop sends the doctor a proposed step from home readings, approved without a visit.
99	- A reading trusted enough to act on, so the "controlled or not" rule [D3-05-F08] can run at home.
100	- It answers distance and missing guidance, not "no sense of being ill" [D3-05-F07].
101	
102	**What it must borrow:** free 30-day refills [D3-05-F02] or doorstep delivery [D3-05-F14]; a person who follows up [D3-05-F03]; the protocol [D3-05-F01]; a doctor's sign-off [D3-05-F30].
103	
104	**Closest precedent:** IMPACT-BP, with home cuffs, delivered medicine and remote nurse decisions [D3-05-F27]. Warnings: visit-time prompts added nothing [D1-01-F46], and China's gain came with drugs and incentives [D1-01-F38].
105	
106	### What we could not find
107	
108	- Any order letting a CHO or nurse change a dose; the national NCD guidelines text.
109	- IHCI full cost per patient; Maharashtra's titrator; an effect size for nurse calls.
110	- Tamil Nadu's delivering cadre and refill interval; who exactly changed doses in IMPACT-BP; Kerala control outcomes.
111	- An Indian decentralised-refill pilot with numbers; China's programme cost; INTE-COMM results; an ECHO India effect on control [D3-05-F33].

1	## E. The engineer's view
2	
3	### What this part shows
4	
5	This part names, for each stage of a therapy loop, the technology that exists in November 2026, its cost and testing, and what a student team can build by noon. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.
6	
7	### The parts of a therapy loop
8	
9	A loop that changes treatment has six stages.
10	
11	| Stage | Its job | Technology found | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| Sense | Get a number from the patient's home | Omron cuffs read with omblepy [D1-06-F07]; cuff-screen photo readers [D2-02-F4]; Bluetooth glucose profile [D1-06-F29] | Photo of any cuff, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
14	| Check the reading | Was it taken properly? | AHA and ESH home rules [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11]; posture-error trials [D2-02-F16] | Kit-built motion clip plus a checklist |
15	| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed next step | Step protocols [D1-06-F14]; HL7 CQL [D2-03-F52]; OpenAPS bounds [D2-03-F46] | One YAML file per protocol, run by a pure `decide()` function |
16	| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | CDS Hooks cards with an accept button [D2-03-F53] | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
17	| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram bot [D2-01-F9]; Indian speech APIs [D2-03-F58] | Telegram chat plus a web form |
18	| Learn | Improve choices from each patient's response | Personal drug-response trials [D2-03-F12]; adaptive message timing [D2-03-F10] | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |
19	
20	![System map of the blood-pressure step loop from home reading to approved change](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)
21	*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*
22	
23	So what for us (OUR VIEW): every stage has open parts and none needs a new model tonight. The value is in joining them with a safety rule at each handover.
24	
25	### Sensing at home in India
26	
27	What a household or maker kit can measure tonight, how the number gets out, and what accuracy studies say. Night delivery to Sonipat was NOT FOUND.
28	
29	| Signal | Device | Price (date) | How data gets out | Accuracy evidence |
30	|---|---|---|---|---|
31	| Blood pressure | Omron HEM-7156T (Bluetooth) | ₹2,593-2,892 (listings to mid-2026, search summary only) [D1-06-F31] | Omron's own protocol, not the standard service; read with omblepy [D1-06-F07, D2-02-F1] | Maker's table cites ISO and ESH grades (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-02-F29] |
32	| Blood pressure | Omron HEM-7120 | RRP ₹2,334 (undated); ₹1,849 online, 10 Jun 2026 (search summary only) [D2-02-F30] | Photo or typing | Passed ESH-IP 2010 (Medaval) [D2-02-F28] |
33	| Blood pressure | Dr Morepen BP-01 | NOT RESEARCHED | Photo or typing | "has not been clinically validated" (Medaval) [D2-02-F32] |
34	| Glucose | Accu-Chek Instant (Bluetooth) | ₹1,124-1,321 (undated, search summary only) [D1-06-F48] | Certified Bluetooth glucose meter; one paired device; third-party reading not confirmed [D1-06-F48] | NOT RESEARCHED |
35	| Pulse, oxygen | MAX30102 (kit) | In kit | I2C to ESP32 | No large independent validation (search summary only) [D1-06-F19] |
36	| Heart rhythm | AD8232 (kit) | In kit | Analog to ESP32 | No human validation found (search summary only) [D1-06-F47] |
37	| Arm position | MPU6050 (kit) | ₹144-275 (undated, search summary only) [D2-02-F31] | I2C to ESP32 | NOT RESEARCHED |
38	| Lung function | ESP32 Venturi spirometer, about £45 | Parts | Python, no repository | n = 30: FEV1 error 5.18%; peak flow error 18.01%, 51.80 L/min too low [D1-06-F24] |
39	| Movement, pulse, walking | Phone only: MediaPipe Pose (33 body points) [D1-06-F26]; camera pulse with pyVHR, GPL-3 [D1-06-F45]; 6-minute walk app | Free | Phone | Walk distance r = 0.83, n = 32 (search summary only) [D1-06-F52]; others NOT RESEARCHED |

41	**Bluetooth in practice.** The standard blood-pressure service is 0x1810 (search summary only) [D1-06-F09], but no India-sold cuff was confirmed to use it [D2-02-F3]. Two Omron Connect models are encrypted [D1-06-F07]. Web Bluetooth needs HTTPS and a user click and is marked experimental [D1-06-F46].
42	
43	**Reading any cuff's screen from a photo.** A purpose-trained reader reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images and 0.9/0.5 mmHg on 1,934 Guatemalan recordings, against 4.1/2.7 mmHg for human transcribers on the Guatemalan set [D2-02-F4]. But 82% of 7,205 images in another Guatemalan set were poor quality, errors sat in the last digit, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. The open tool ssocr reads one row of digits [D2-02-F7]; 0 and 8, 1 and 7 get confused (search summary only) [D2-02-F9]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8].
44	
45	**Blood pressure without a cuff, as of 2026.** The FDA cleared the Aktiia G0 cuffless monitor on 2 Jul 2025 [D2-02-F23]. The ESH says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25], and a 2025 review found "no compelling evidence" of added value from pulse-wave methods [D2-02-F26]. A cuff must agree within a mean of 5 mmHg, SD up to 8 (search summary only) [D2-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, and a kit version cannot be validated by noon. Do not build it tonight.
46	
47	So what for us (OUR VIEW): blood pressure is the one signal a household can measure tonight with a validated, cheap device. The photo path reaches any cuff, so we do not depend on Bluetooth, but every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.
48	
49	### Making a home reading trustworthy
50	
51	A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff. This section gives the guidance, the size of each mistake, the home threshold, and the clip that catches what a sensor can see.
52	
53	**The guidance.** AHA: at least 5 minutes of quiet seated rest, two readings at least 1 minute apart, morning before tablets and evening, 7 days or more (minimum 3) [D2-02-F10]. ESH: the same, "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Dropping day 1 is "a matter of debate" for the ESH [D2-02-F12]; the AHA notes some guidelines drop it [D2-02-F10]. The ESH warns monitors over 4 years old drift [D2-02-F13] and calls handwritten logs "often incomplete and inaccurate" [D2-02-F14].
54	
55	**The size of each mistake** (systolic / diastolic, mmHg):
56	
57	| Mistake | Effect | Source |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| Arm on lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover, n = 133, Baltimore) | [D2-02-F16] |
60	| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) | [D2-02-F16] |
61	| Arm below heart level | +0.49 / +0.47 per cm; arm at desk height against heart height +6.1 / +5.7 (n = 128) | [D2-02-F17] |
62	| Back not supported | +5 to +15 / +6 (AHA); +6 to +10 systolic (older table) | [D2-02-F18, D2-02-F20] |
63	| Legs crossed | +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 | [D2-02-F18] |
64	| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large one | +4.8 systolic (randomised crossover, n = 195) | [D2-02-F19] |
65	| Regular cuff on an arm that needs an extra-large one | +19.5 systolic | [D2-02-F19] |
66	| Talking | +10 / +10 (older table, no citations in it) | [D2-02-F20] |
67	| Cuff over clothing | +5 to +50 systolic (older table) | [D2-02-F20] |
68	| No rest instead of 5 minutes | No meaningful difference below 140 systolic; none to at least 4 mmHg above (secondary review) | [D2-02-F21] |
69	
70	The HEM-7120 standard cuff fits arms of 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30], so arm size must be measured.
71	
72	**Home against clinic thresholds.** The ESH says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the ISH [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines on Hypertension IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use 135/85 at home. The Gujarat protocol is written for clinic readings at 140/90 [D1-06-F14]. Our engine (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-01-F1]) measures on days 24-30 of each 30-day cycle, counts a session only if both readings pass the quality check, needs 3 valid days, drops day 1 only when 4 or more remain, calls the block "still high" at a mean of 135 or 85, and sends any confirmed session at 180 or 110 to urgent review. Using a clinic protocol on home readings is our choice and must be said on the slide.
73	
74	Why it matters: SMARThealth India (stepped-wedge cluster trial, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].
75	
76	**The kit-built quality clip** (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F16, D2-02-F17]). An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff and the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once and the clip stores that posture. It then enforces 300 seconds of still rest (restarting on movement), checks the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture, requires stillness through a 60-second measurement, and enforces 60 seconds between readings. A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2). It shows green or red and posts reasons, joined to the reading by time. Legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, bladder and smoking go into a 4-question phone checklist. Thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE.
77	
78	![The reading-quality clip on the upper arm and forearm, with its green and red states](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)
79	*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*
80	
81	So what for us (OUR VIEW): the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.
82	
83	### Algorithms that set a dose
84	
85	Four families of dose algorithm are in use; each is bounded.
86	
87	**Closed-loop insulin, the model case.** Control-IQ (randomised 2:1, 168 people with type 1 diabetes, USA, 6 months, against a sensor-augmented pump) raised time in the target glucose range by 11 points and cut HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) by 0.33, with one ketoacidosis case [D1-01-F24]. In insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, 2IQP (randomised 2:1, 319 adults, US and Canada, 13 weeks, both arms on a glucose sensor, maker-funded) cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points [D1-01-F43]. The do-it-yourself system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down [D2-03-F46]:
88	- It acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the core version "cannot issue insulin boluses".
89	- The temporary rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate".
90	- Missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan.
91	
92	Its code (oref0, MIT) says it is "not a 'set and forget' system" [D1-06-F12]; dosing logic sits in `determine-basal.js` [D1-06-F53].
93	
94	**Insulin titration rules.** ADA 2025: start basal insulin at 10 units a day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, "increase 2 units every 3 days to reach FPG target without hypoglycemia", and if low sugar has no clear reason "lower dose by 10-20%" [D1-06-F16]. An upper limit of 0.5 units/kg/day is quoted (search summary only) [D1-06-F18]. India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. d-Nav (randomised, 181 adults with type 2 diabetes, 3 US centres, 6 months, device plus clinician against clinician alone) cut HbA1c 1.0% against 0.3% with equal low-sugar events; several authors were maker staff or shareholders [D1-01-F13]. TeleDiab-2 (randomised, 191 adults starting basal insulin, France, 4 months) cut HbA1c 1.44% and 1.48% against 0.92% [D1-01-F14]. The FDA has cleared dose apps such as My Dose Coach (2017) and iSage Rx (2024) [D2-03-F47]. A reinforcement-learning model, RL-DITR, was tested only single-arm in 16 inpatients in China [D2-03-F11].
95	
96	**Blood-pressure protocols.** Gujarat's ladder, with 30-day reviews: amlodipine 5 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, add telmisartan 40 mg, telmisartan 80 mg (after blood sugar, urea, creatinine and urine protein; if any is abnormal, refer, or, with no specialist reachable, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone), add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, then check adherence and refer; the sheet covers adults over 30, checks adherence at each visit, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception [D1-06-F14]. Punjab and Maharashtra differ at step 2 [D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]; across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82% [D1-06-F04]. People do differ: PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden, 1,468 treatment periods) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if chosen per person [D2-03-F12]. A one-time "responder" label from a short run-in did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13].
97	
98	**Warfarin tables.** The IWPC algorithm sets only the starting dose [D2-03-F48]. Feedback tables agree on no change at INR (a clotting test) 2.0-3.0 but differ outside it (search summary only) [D1-06-F37]. Self-management cut clots (RR 0.47) and deaths (RR 0.55) in pooled trials, compared indirectly with self-testing [D1-02-F05].
99	
100	| Algorithm | Input | Output | How it is bounded |
101	|---|---|---|---|
102	| Closed-loop insulin | Continuous glucose sensor | Temporary basal rate | Rate caps, no boluses (oref0), revert on missing data [D2-03-F46] |
103	| Basal titration | Fasting glucose over 3 days | +2 units or -10-20% | Upper limit per kg; hypo branch; clinician sets cause [D1-06-F16, D1-06-F18] |
104	| BP ladder | 30-day review of readings | Next written regimen | Fixed steps, lab and pregnancy guards, referral at the end [D1-06-F14] |
105	| Warfarin table | INR | Weekly dose change in % | No-change band 2.0-3.0; hold at high INR [D1-06-F37] |
106	
107	So what for us (OUR VIEW): every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing. A ladder is the simplest case. PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.

109	### A protocol as data
110	
111	A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch, and swapped without changing the engine. This section gives the prior art, what Indian decision-support trials found, and how our files fit.
112	
113	**Prior art.** A 2002 review of 11 guideline languages found four basic parts: data collection, decision, patient state, intervention [D2-03-F54]. WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit; the blood-pressure kit is for pregnancy only, its machine-readable layers are "not yet available", and its licence is non-commercial [D2-03-F50, D2-03-F51]. HL7 CQL is a standard logic language with an Apache-2.0 engine that is "not a complete implementation" and needs a Java 17 translator [D2-03-F52]. CDS Hooks returns suggestion cards with an accept button (CC BY 4.0) [D2-03-F53]. India's open Simple app (MIT, alive 4 Nov 2026) stores a protocol as a drug list plus `follow_up_days`; no step logic was found in its protocol model [D1-06-F40].
114	
115	**Indian decision-support trials.**
116	
117	| Trial | Design and setting | Compared | Result |
118	|---|---|---|---|
119	| CARRS [D2-03-F14] | Randomised, 1,146 with diabetes, urban clinics, India and Pakistan, 28 months | Coordinators plus decision-support records against usual care | Positive: composite goal 18.2% against 8.1% |
120	| mWellcare [D2-03-F15] | Cluster randomised, 40 health centres, 3,698 people, 12 months | Nurse-run app with decision support against enhanced usual care | Null: systolic -0.98 (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67) |
121	| mPower Heart [D2-03-F16] | Before-and-after, no control, Himachal Pradesh, 6,797 people | Phone tool drafts prescription, physician vets | Systolic -14.6 mmHg, uncontrolled |
122	| SMARThealth India [D2-03-F17] | Stepped-wedge cluster, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh | Health-worker tablet plus doctor decision support against usual care | Null on blood pressure |
123	| IMPACT Diabetes [D2-03-F18] | Cluster randomised, 8 centres, 418 people, 9 months | Health-worker decision support under physician supervision | Small positive: HbA1c fall of 0.5% or more, 21.8% against 10.3% |
124	
125	**The test-coverage lesson.** When the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].
126	
127	**How our files fit** (OUR DESIGN, detail in part J). One YAML file per protocol (Gujarat, Nigeria, and the ADA insulin rule as paper only), each number carrying the exact source words; a missing value is `null` and the engine refuses that branch [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15, D1-06-F16]. A pure `decide()` function checks safety first, then enough readings, the 30-day interval, the threshold, adherence, the last step, and the lab and pregnancy guards, and only then proposes a step. It never computes a dose; it only picks a regimen written in the file. Thirty-six test cases cover every branch listed so far, run against two protocols; the age, childbearing-age, abnormal-lab and "outside the demo" branches found later on the sheets still need tests (part J) [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15].
128	
129	So what for us (OUR VIEW): decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so our engine must act between visits, not prompt during them. ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.

131	### Adaptive nudging, bandits and reinforcement learning
132	
133	Adaptive nudging learns when and what to send each person. A just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) adapts "weekly, daily, or even many times a day"; a micro-randomised trial randomises each decision point [D2-03-F01].
134	
135	| Study | Design | Result |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| HeartSteps V1 [D2-03-F02] | Micro-randomised, 44 US adults, 6 weeks | Any suggestion +35 steps in 30 minutes (p = .06), fading over time; walking suggestions +59 (p = .02) |
138	| HeartSteps V2 [D2-03-F03]; Oralytics [D2-03-F08] | Learning algorithms deployed in US trials | Outcome results NOT FOUND |
139	| DIAMANTE [D2-03-F10] | Randomised, 3 arms, 168 people with diabetes and depression, US safety-net clinics, 6 months | Learned texts beat random texts: steps up 19% against 1.6% (random) and 3.9% (weekly message); HbA1c not in the abstract |
140	| Automated diabetes prevention app [D2-03-F42] | Randomised non-inferiority, 368 people, 2 US sites, 12 months | Matched human coaches: 31.7% against 31.9% |
141	| JITAI meta-analyses [D2-03-F04, D2-03-F06] | Mental health, 23 studies; sleep, 11 trials | Small effect (g = 0.15); adaptive not better than non-adaptive for sleep |
142	
143	Two cautions. Standard estimators "can be inconsistent and fail to be replicable" on bandit-trial data [D2-03-F09]. A 2026 guideline for live learning systems uses pre-set fallbacks, which "safeguarded participants" in two case studies [D2-03-F07].
144	
145	Open tools: MABWiser (Apache 2.0) [D1-06-F55]; Open Bandit Pipeline (Apache 2.0, off-policy estimators) [D2-03-F49]; HeartSteps V1 data (CC BY 4.0, 8,274 decisions) [D1-06-F44].
146	
147	So what for us (OUR VIEW): adaptive timing has one head-to-head win, on steps, not a clinical measure. In our loop it could help complete 7-day reading blocks, later. A HeartSteps replay shows the method only.
148	
149	### Personal response models and "digital twins"
150	
151	A "digital twin" here is a model of one person that predicts their response to food or treatment.
152	
153	- **Twin Health, India, blood pressure** [D2-03-F19]: secondary analysis of an Indian randomised trial in 319 people with type 2 diabetes (233 twin, 86 standard care). Home readings guided blood-pressure drug changes. Systolic fell 7.6 against 3.2 mmHg at one year. Limits: secondary analysis, only 59 people on blood-pressure drugs, company-linked. The drug changes followed a protocol; the machine learning predicted diet response.
154	- **Method** [D2-03-F21]: predicts each person's post-meal glucose from a glucose sensor, food logs and other inputs and "dynamically adjusts dietary recommendations". No open code found.
155	- **Twin Health, US** [D2-03-F43]: randomised, 150 people, Cleveland Clinic, 12 months; HbA1c under 6.5% without glucose drugs other than metformin in 71% against 2.4%. Source is the institution's summary; funding not shown.
156	- **Twin Health, real world** [D2-03-F20]: 1,853 completers, HbA1c -1.8%, no control (THEIR CLAIM).
157	- **Glucose foundation models**: GluFormer (over 10 million readings, 10,812 adults) predicted later diabetes and cardiovascular death (arXiv only) [D2-03-F23]; CGM-LSM and GlucoFM report lower forecast error [D2-03-F24].
158	- **Blood pressure**: one agent-based model simulates six drugs on virtual patients; licence unconfirmed (search summary only) [D1-06-F43].
159	
160	PHYSIC measured personal response over repeated periods [D2-03-F12]; a single run-in response did not predict the long-term one [D2-03-F13].
161	
162	So what for us (OUR VIEW): no open twin exists for blood-pressure drugs. Each approved step in our loop gives one labelled example (readings before, readings 30 days after). That is the dataset a response model would need, and it does not exist in the open today [D1-06-F42].

184	### Language models and medicine doses
185	
186	Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol.
187	
188	| Study | Setup | Error |
189	|---|---|---|
190	| TacroDose AI [D2-03-F38] | GPT-4 prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol, 300 simulated cases | First version: 13.9% "sentinel errors"; with stronger constraints and output checks: 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) |
191	| Anticoagulant hold times [D2-03-F39] | ChatGPT and Gemini, 25 cases | "potentially dangerous recommendations in 12-20% of scenarios" |
192	| Prescribing-error checker [D2-03-F40] | Randomised crossover, 91 error scenarios | Pharmacist plus model was best, 61% accuracy; 1.5 times better than the pharmacist alone at catching serious errors |
193	| Incident-report classification [D2-03-F41] | o4-mini, 200 Swedish reports | 96.0% agreement with pharmacists |
194	
195	No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44], and an Indian trial protocol uses a frozen Mistral-7B with nurses after heart surgery [D2-03-F37].
196	
197	**The design pattern** (OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]):
198	1. The model handles language only: cuff photo to strict JSON, translation, speech.
199	2. A fixed, tested engine makes every decision, from the protocol file.
200	3. Code checks every output against the protocol: plausible ranges, two agreeing reads, a regimen that exists in the file.
201	4. A clinician approves every change.

270	### So what for us
271	
272	OUR VIEW.
273	- **The reading is the science.** Arm position alone adds 3.9-6.5 mmHg [D2-02-F16], and noisy readings broke an Indian trial [D2-03-F17]. The clip and reading rules are our deep-tech claim, not the rules engine.
274	- **Bound every action.** Copy OpenAPS [D2-03-F46]: choose only written regimens, hold the current step on missing data, never step on one reading.
275	- **Keep models on language.** A constrained model still made dangerous dose errors 1% of the time [D2-03-F38]; it reads photos and speaks Hindi, and the engine decides.
276	- **Act between visits, not during them.** Decision support used during clinic visits did not beat good usual care in India [D2-03-F15, D2-03-F17]; our value is the change made without a visit.
277	- **The learning layer is earned, not claimed.** People do respond differently to drugs [D2-03-F12], but no open data exists to model it; each approved step we log builds it.

177	### The gap
178	
179	OUR VIEW. No Indian service was found that turns home BP or glucose readings into a medicine change between visits [D1-04-F09, D1-04-F19]. Indian programmes stop at coaching or reminders [D1-04-F02, D1-06-F40]. Abroad the space is held by US programmes paid by US payers [D1-05-F13, D1-05-F46]; the low-income-country programmes found are protocol care, not device-linked dose loops [D1-05-F65]. The closest abroad: Closed Loop Medicine (UK) has been in members' voluntary liquidation since 28 Apr 2026 [D3-06-F07], its website now points to a licensing firm [D3-06-F08], and its one trial had no comparison group (205 patients, systolic down 11 mmHg) [D3-06-F09]; Cadence's protocol-bound titration software entered a US regulator's (FDA) pilot on 13 Aug 2026 and is not cleared (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F31]; and Omron, the Japanese cuff maker, has a UK product that drafts a medication plan for the clinician to accept or modify (search summary only) [D3-06-F35]. These are one night's search results: a hospital, drug maker or state may run something unpublished.
180	
181	### So what for us
182	
183	OUR VIEW.
184	- **Stand where nobody was found:** a home BP loop that proposes the next protocol step for a doctor to approve, the only kind of programme PHTI passed [D1-05-F2].
185	- **Sell to a payer, not a patient.** Pear, Akili and Better Therapeutics had trials yet failed for lack of payment [D1-05-F20, D1-02-F44, D1-02-F46].
186	- **Build the prescriber in.** Clinician referral adds 40 days of retention [D1-02-F27]; Pear lacked prescribers [D1-05-F21].
187	- **Never sell the sensor or the reminder as the product,** and keep spending in line with revenue [D1-02-F41, D1-04-F23].
188	- **Measure what payers count from day one:** share under 140/90, and how many lost patients return [D1-05-F31].

157	### 10. The rules in India
158	
159	These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO (the national medical-device regulator).
160	
161	**(a) Software as a medical device.** CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" (CDSCO/MD/GD/MDSW/01/2026) on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. Class follows the intended use, as stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. Its grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:
162	
163	| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
164	|---|---|---|---|
165	| Critical | D | C | B |
166	| Serious | C | B | A |
167	| Non-serious | B | A | A |
168	
169	"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" and support for "safe and effective use of medicinal products" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits, so the class turns on that grading [D2-04-F05]. A patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical" [D2-04-F03]. CDSCO names a hypertension digital therapeutics platform and a Bluetooth cuff app as medical device software, and bars the wellness carve-out once a disease is named [D2-04-F07, D2-04-F09]. Unlike the US, there is no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. CDSCO confirms the class on review [D2-04-F06].
170	
171	**(b) A study on patients before a licence.** A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14]; the flowchart notes it is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. A desk test on open data, simulators or teammates is not a clinical investigation; whether a pilot where software drafts and a doctor decides counts as one is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Fees and processing days NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].
172	
173	**(c) Telemedicine.** The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; such tools may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. List B medicines may be added at a follow-up; the guidelines define follow-up as the same doctor, same condition, within 6 months of the previous in-person consultation (clause 3.6.2) [D2-04-F17, D2-01-F10]. Annexure 1 names hypertension examples (List A refills such as enalapril and atenolol; List B add-on of a thiazide diuretic with atenolol); amlodipine, telmisartan and chlorthalidone are not named [D2-04-F17]. The claims check read the official text; whether later rules changed it in 2026 was not checked [D2-04-F17].
174	
175	**(d) Nurse or health officer changing a dose.** In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription"; no titration by them is described [D2-04-F18]. NOT FOUND: any law, rule or ministry order letting a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18].
176	
177	**(e) Claims and advertising.** The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats a disease in its Schedule, which lists "Diabetes", "Heart diseases" and "High or low blood pressure" [D2-04-F31]. Whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested; a question for counsel [D2-04-F31].
178	
179	**(f) Data law.** Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025, consent-manager rules start one year after 13 Nov 2025, on 13 Nov 2026; notice, consent and data-fiduciary duties start 18 months after, on 13 May 2027, by the gazette's wording; one law firm (AZB) says a day earlier, 12 Nov 2026 and 12 May 2027 [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20]. Health data has no general exemption; only children's-data duties are waived for health providers [D2-04-F40].
180	
181	**(g) Ethics and registration.** ICMR's 2023 AI guidelines say humans should keep "complete control" and require consent that names the AI [D2-04-F35]. Trial registration on CTRI is mandatory before first enrolment for trials, with ethics approval uploaded; whether a clinician-decides pilot needs it is NOT FOUND (search summary only) [D2-04-F45].
182	
183	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** Clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.

213	
214	OUR VIEW:
215	- Sell to private clinics and hospital chains first, at about ₹149 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION); patients alone will not pay enough.
216	- The used SAM is ₹749 crore and the US$100 million test fails in India on blood pressure alone (OUR ARITHMETIC), so the pitch is one engine for many protocols and payers.
217	- The Indian pilot must produce control data at 90 days, because insurers, states and German-style outcome pay all ask for it.
218	- Plan for Class B, ask CDSCO for a written class early, and keep the doctor approving every change.
219	- Build data consent to the May 2027 duties now, and say nothing in public about treating blood pressure.

3	### G1. What this part shows
4	
5	This part tests the home blood-pressure step loop as a strategy partner and an early-stage deep-tech investor would: one governing question, the choices, money, forces, risks and the next 90 days. Claims-check corrections (D3-01 to D3-03) are applied; judgements carry OUR VIEW.
6	
7	### G2. The question tree
8	
9	The governing question: "Can a medicine-adjusting loop that starts with blood pressure become a business that improves outcomes for people far from a specialist?" Six sub-questions follow, each graded strong, partial or missing.
10	
11	| Sub-question | What the research supports | Evidence |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| 1. Does the loop work? | Abroad, yes, in randomised trials. US, HyperLink: 450 adults, pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings against usual care, 57.2% against 30.0% controlled at 6 and 12 months [D1-01-F04]. Lesotho: 547 adults, lay workers adjusting one pill with an app against referral to a clinic, 58% against 48% controlled at 12 months [D3-05-F24]. India's nearest trial was null: mWellcare, 3,698 people at 40 health centres, 12 months, a decision-support app at the visit against enhanced usual care, systolic (the upper number) 0.98 mmHg apart, not significant [D1-01-F46]. No Indian randomised trial of the home loop was found (D1-01). | Strong abroad; missing in India |
14	| 2. Is the gap real in India? | Yes. At 24 government-programme clinics 51% of 21,895 registered patients returned; among them control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% (no comparison group) [D1-03-F10]. The cause is less clear: of 157 lapsed patients phoned in Bathinda (not a random sample), 24.8% felt no illness and 22.2% named distance [D3-05-F07]. | Strong on size; partial on cause |
15	| 3. 165	### 7. Eight ideas to borrow for a home blood-pressure step loop
166	
167	OUR VIEW, most useful first.
168	
169	1. Protocol held as data, options with reasons shown to the clinician, response fed back (Closed Loop Medicine) [D2-06-F24].
170	2. Before any step up, a call in the patient's language asks whether the tablet was taken, as the Gujarat protocol requires (Tucuvi) [D2-06-F10, D1-06-F14].
171	3. Report readings closed with no clinician touch and clinician minutes per patient (Cadence) [D2-06-F2].
172	4. Log every accept, edit and reject as the safety and training record (Counsel Health) [D2-06-F11].
173	5. A one-page staged safety ladder: supervised first, wider authority after testing (Hippocratic AI) [D2-06-F20].
174	6. Alert on drift of the 7-day mean, not single readings (Prana) [D2-06-F13].
175	7. One reading schema (value, time, device, quality) for any cuff or watch (Junction) [D2-06-F30].
176	8. Cuffless or 24-hour readings as an input or one-off check only; dose decisions stay on cuff readings (Aktiia, Biobeat) [D2-06-F37, D2-06-F36].

187	#### S.M.A.R.T problem statement
188	
189	To stop blood pressure staying high because the dose change waits for a visit that half the patients never make [R], doctors in private clinics and their patients on blood-pressure medicine [S] need the 30-day review done from home, as a doctor-approved next step of the published protocol [A], shown in one clinic over a 90-day pilot [T], measured by the share of patients under 140/90 and bought at ₹149 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION) [M].
190	
191	- **S · Specific:** one buyer (a hypothesis) and one gap: the dose step between visits.
192	- **M · Measurable:** the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned. The price is an ASSUMPTION.
193	- **A · Action-oriented:** each cycle ends in one action: step up, support, order tests, refer or hold.
194	- **R · Relevant:** 51% returned; control among them rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
195	- **T · Time-bound:** a prototype by noon on 14 November 2026; a pilot endpoint at 90 days.
196	
197	#### The belief we turn upside down
198	
199	- **Belief we turn over:** a medicine dose can change only when the patient is in front of the doctor.
200	- **Instead:** the reading travels to the doctor and the decision travels home. The 30-day review happens whether or not the patient returns.
201	
202	Why we think this solves the problem (OUR VIEW):
203	
204	- The step that fails in India is the return visit, not the protocol [D1-03-F10].
205	- Where the dose changed without a clinic visit, pressure fell [D1-01-F02, D1-01-F04].
206	- Readings alone do not do it: pooled across 15 trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring alone gave 1.0 mmHg against usual care, no effect [D1-01-F05].
207	- The limit: prompting a clinician during a visit added nothing in mWellcare [D1-01-F46], so the value must come between visits.
