28	On about 2 Jun 2026 he posted an invitation to a "DeepTech Open Mic" for health and biotech builders at IIT Madras Research Park on 4 Jun 2026: five early founders, an 8-minute pitch with no slides, then 7 minutes of feedback on narrative and positioning ([his LinkedIn activity](https://www.linkedin.com/in/karthikvarada/recent-activity/all/), read 13 Nov 2026). He wrote that deep-tech builders need low-pressure places to practise their story. The readings disagree: one recorded every item in his feed as a repost [D2-07-F10], the other recorded this invitation as his own post.
29	
30	So what for us. OUR VIEW: tell the whole loop in 8 minutes without slides: patient, reading, dose step, clinician approval, outcome.
31	
32	### The fund
33	
34	- **What it backs.** Founders solving social issues with deep science and deep tech, pre-seed to Series A, lab to market; health and biotech sit in its "life infrastructure" area ([fund's India page](https://beyondnextventures.com/india/)).
35	- **The India fund.** India 1 Investment Partnership, its first fund only for Indian deep tech. First deal: Volt14 (battery cells), 14 May 2025, a US$1.87M round led by Blume, the fund participating ([fund's release](https://beyondnextventures.com/news/beyond-next-ventures-volt14)). Second: FinalLayer (AI video), amount undisclosed ([Entrepreneur India, 27 Oct 2025](https://india.entrepreneur.com/news-and-trends/beyond-next-ventures-invests-in-ai-startup-finallayer/498777)); the fund page dates it 23 Oct 2025 [D2-07-F9].
36	- **Registration.** The India trust is registered with SEBI as a Category II Alternative Investment Fund [D2-07-F11].
37	- **Japan-India link.** The India arm hosts a talk on Japan's "Physical AI" startups on 18 Nov 2026 [D2-07-F11]; a 3 Dec 2026 Tokyo event with Intralink on Japanese companies working with Indian startups names healthcare among its sectors ([fund's India LinkedIn posts](https://www.linkedin.com/company/beyond-next-ventures-india/posts/), read 13 Nov 2026).
38	- **Why a Delhi-NCR campus.** The India arm hired a Delhi-NCR operator for university pre-incubation and campus events [D2-07-F17] and partnered with IILM University on pre-incubation [D2-07-F16]. His link to SPARK Night rests on the poster only; the event site did not list him on 12 Nov 2026 ([event site](https://techsparks.org)).
39	
40	So what for us. OUR VIEW: Ashoka sits inside a campus funnel the fund builds on purpose; a team with a working prototype is its pipeline.
41	
42	### The fund's health record
43	
44	| Item | What the notes say | Status |
45	|---|---|---|
46	| Biomoneta | Airborne-infection control for hospitals; reports US FDA 510(k) clearance for "Avata Rx" [D2-07-F12, D2-07-F13] | Portfolio verified; clearance THEIR CLAIM |
47	| MediBuddy, ImpactGuru, Generic Aadhaar, MEDFIN, TruDoc | Older, non-deep-tech India holdings ([fund's India page](https://beyondnextventures.com/india/)) | Listed by the fund |
48	| CarePal / ImpactGuru | Health financing; about 70% of India's middle class lacks health insurance [D2-07-F15] | Figure THEIR CLAIM |
49	| Wellthy Therapeutics | Indian digital-therapy company, labelled "acquired by TruDoc" on LinkedIn [D2-07-F19] | The fund led Wellthy's financing announced on 15 June 2023, amount not disclosed [D3-06-F01] |
50	| SCOHIA PHARMA | Japanese drug discovery for metabolic, endocrine and cardiovascular disease, about Jun 2026 ([fund's India LinkedIn posts](https://www.linkedin.com/company/beyond-next-ventures-india/posts/)) Its programme SCO-240 was selected, about Sep 2026, for a drug-discovery venture scheme of AMED (the Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development) that subsidises two thirds of eligible costs ([fund's Tokyo LinkedIn posts](https://www.linkedin.com/company/beyond-next-ventures/posts/), read 13 Nov 2026). | Fund's announcement |
51	| Anaut | AI reading of endoscopic images in surgery; UKCA mark (UK product-conformity mark), Jun 2026 (same page) | Fund repost |
52	| Aillis | Medical AI company; one of three portfolio companies recognised at the Japan Startup Awards 2026, about Oct 2026 ([fund's Tokyo LinkedIn posts](https://www.linkedin.com/company/beyond-next-ventures/posts/), read 13 Nov 2026) | Fund's post |
53	| Panasonic Ignition 3.0 | Fund continues as venture partner (3 Sep 2025) [D2-07-F9]; "health and wellness" is a theme ([Jay Krishnan's LinkedIn activity](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thejaykrishnan/recent-activity/all/)) | Verified |
54	| CII healthcare delegation | Tokyo firm hosted Indian health executives about a year ago; named telemedicine, diagnostics and medtech for partnership (same page) | Partner's repost |
55	| RayIoT | Wi-Fi breathing and sleep sensing in Panasonic air-conditioners; he congratulated the founder [D2-07-F20] | Portfolio status NOT VERIFIED |
56	
57	About three years ago, under the Wellthy founder's post on its FDA quality-system and HIPAA certifications, he wrote: "This truly broadens the scope for number of patients that Wellthy can serve! Congratulations!!" [D2-07-F19].
58	
59	So what for us. OUR VIEW: the record shows device clearances and financing, not a dose-changing therapy; our loop would be new.
60	
61	#### Added from a second LinkedIn reading (13 Nov 2026, about 10:25 PM)
62	
63	These items come from the fund's and companies' own LinkedIn pages, recorded in `research_notes\dtx\L2-linkedin-players-fund-health.md`. Company figures are THEIR CLAIM.
64	
65	- **A live case of measurement guiding treatment in the fund's portfolio.** Universal Brain received a US FDA 510(k) clearance, about August 2026, for an EEG-based brain-function measurement used in psychiatry. It is starting studies in the US and Japan on markers of response to antidepressants, and began clinical use about mid-October 2026 (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026). OUR VIEW: this is the nearest thing in the portfolio to the challenge's "biomarkers to personalise care", and it shows the fund backs products that carry a regulator's clearance.
66	- **Wellthy.** LinkedIn alone shows no post linking the fund to Wellthy. The open-web check settles it: see the next block.
67	- **Nothing on digital therapeutics.** No post on digital therapeutics, or on Japan's prescription-app companies, appeared in the 30 Tokyo posts that loaded.
68	- **Two field voices worth knowing before the pitch** (paraphrased; numbers inside the posts are unverified). A national NCD consultant at UNICEF India wrote, about April 2026, that what broke programmes on the ground was blood-pressure machines left uncalibrated for months and medicines running out mid-month. A doctor who works as a WHO consultant wrote, about October 2026, that counting registrations and visits is not enough, and cited the mWellcare trial as proof that a digital system alone does not improve control. OUR VIEW: both points are already in this document's argument (trust the reading; the dose change is the active part), and the mentor's circle is likely to know them.
69	
70	#### Added from the open-web check (13 Nov 2026, about 10:30 PM)
71	
72	- **The fund led a round in an Indian digital-therapeutics company, and the mentor is named in the release.** Wellthy Therapeutics announced on 15 June 2023 "additional financing" led by Beyond Next Ventures, amount not disclosed, to fund expansion into Japan. The release carries a joint quote from Yuichiro Sano and Karthik Varada saying the firm has "invested in many cutting-edge digital health ventures across India and Japan" [D3-06-F01]. The fund's India page today lists TruDoc, which bought Wellthy in February 2024, and not Wellthy [D3-06-F03].
73	- **The fund's first investment was Japan's prescription-app company.** The fund's chief executive wrote on 7 October 2024 that CureApp was the first investment from its first fund in 2015 (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F26]. CureApp's blood-pressure app has been covered by Japan's health insurance since 1 September 2022. It supports lifestyle change and does not change medicines [D3-06-F19]. From 1 June 2026 a clinic is paid 90 points a month in person or 78 online for managing it, plus 7,010 yen for the app [D3-06-F20]. In its trial the app lowered 24-hour systolic pressure by 2.4 mmHg more than advice alone [D1-01-F07].
74	- **A Japanese cuff maker already sells the nearest product, in the UK.** Omron's Hypertension Plus, licensed from the University of Oxford, is reported to collect home readings and draft a medication plan that the clinician accepts or modifies (search summary only; Omron's own pages could not be opened) [D3-06-F35].
75	- **A warning from the same field.** Closed Loop Medicine, a UK company that adjusted amlodipine doses through an app, entered members' voluntary liquidation on 28 April 2026 [D3-06-F07]. Its one trial had no comparison group: 205 patients, systolic pressure down 11 mmHg over 14 weeks [D3-06-F09].
76	
77	OUR VIEW. This changes how to frame the pitch. The fund has backed a lifestyle-only blood-pressure app in Japan and a coaching-led programme in India. The home step loop is the piece neither had: the reading changes the medicine. Say that plainly, and be ready for the question the Wellthy story raises, which is who pays.
78	
79	### What we do not know
80	
81	- Any statement by him on digital therapeutics, chronic disease or hypertension. Neither reading found one [D2-07-F10].
82	- The judges, judging criteria or scoring. Nothing read mentions SPARK Night.
83	- Any cheque size or fund size. Nothing read states one.
84	- Whether RayIoT is a portfolio company. (Whether the fund backed Wellthy directly is now answered: it did, as lead, in June 2023 [D3-06-F01].)
85	
86	### How to frame the home blood-pressure step loop for him
87	
88	OUR VIEW, five points:
89	
90	1. **One outcome, measured one way.** Share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned (51% return today) [D1-03-F10]; a US review counted a 5 mmHg systolic fall as meaningful [D1-01-F39]. Show how each home reading is checked for posture and repeats.
91	2. **The easiest wedge.** His partner asks for the "easiest" wedge into a large market [D2-07-F14]. Blood pressure is it: 35.5% of Indian adults 20 and over [D1-03-F01], a cuff at about ₹2,600 (search summary only) [D1-06-F31], and a step protocol already in government text [D1-06-F14]. The same engine loads an insulin protocol next.
92	3. **Prototype to product.** Tonight: every protocol branch tested, a clinician approving each change. Next: a 90-day pilot. The partner says investors like to enter between an alpha prototype and a beta customer pilot ([Jay Krishnan's LinkedIn activity](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thejaykrishnan/recent-activity/all/)).
93	4. **A real Japan angle.** Name only Panasonic's health and wellness theme [D2-07-F9], the CII delegation and the Intralink event. Claim no Japanese partner.
94	5. **Say the null result first.** In mWellcare, a cluster trial of 3,698 people at 40 Indian health centres, a nurse decision-support app made no difference against enhanced usual care: 0.98 mmHg (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67) [D1-01-F46]. Our loop works between visits, where that trial did not look.
95	
96	### Five questions to expect
97	
98	| Question | Honest answer |
99	|---|---|
100	| What outcome changes, by how much? | In HyperLink, pharmacist titration from home readings gave 57.2% controlled against 30.0% at 6 months [D1-01-F04]. We have no patient data of our own. |
101	| Is this just a rules engine? | The hard parts are trusting a home reading and telling a missed dose from a needed step-up; adherence tools alone failed [D1-02-F59]. |
102	| Who pays? | Not known yet. Firms selling an app alone died [D1-02-F42]. |
103	| Is it safe and legal? | A clinician approves every change; unsafe cases go up. The regulatory class is still open. |
104	| Will patients stay? | Clinician referral adds 40 days of retention [D1-02-F27]; only 63.6% of women own a phone, so it must work on a shared one [D1-03-F42]. |
105	
106	### Five questions worth asking him
107	
108	1. Your fund led Wellthy's 2023 round and Wellthy now sits inside TruDoc: who ended up paying for that kind of chronic-disease programme, and what would you do differently?
109	2. What evidence would you want before a pilot: 90-day control, or something harder?
110	3. Does anyone in the Panasonic programme or the CII corridor work on home measurement?
111	4. How does the campus pre-incubation route work, and can an Ashoka team enter it?
112	5. Could Biomoneta or Anaut share how they handled device approval?

1	# SPARK Night 2026: the adaptive care challenge, told as one story
2	
3	**What this is.** The working document for the Beyond Next Ventures challenge at SPARK Night (13-14 Nov 2026, Ashoka University), rewritten on 14 November so that it reads in one line from start to finish. It is the same research as the 13 November edition, in a new order. Nothing was researched again, no fact was changed and nothing was added. Repeated passages were removed, and each topic now sits in one place. Internal to the team.
4	
5	**Status.** The research was completed on 13 Nov 2026 at about 11:10 PM. Three claims checks re-opened the sources of about 183 load-bearing facts, and their corrections are applied throughout. Chapter 7 says what was not checked and what was not found.
6	
7	**The challenge, as set by the fund.**
8	
9	> We need ways to manage chronic disease burden at scale despite limited access to resources, specialists and irregular clinical follow-ups. Patients need treatment methods that responds to their specific condition, and will remain adaptive to patient needs between appointments. How can digital therapeutics use rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers to continuously personalise care, thereby bringing measurable improvements in health outcomes to patients who cannot access frequent specialist support? The opportunity is to extend effective treatment into everyday life, beyond monitoring and reminders.
10	
11	### How the document is laid out
12	
13	The story comes first, in the order the argument builds. The answer comes at the end of the story, not at the start. The appendix holds the full detail behind each chapter, each topic in one place.
14	
15	| Chapter | The question it answers | Full detail in |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| 1. The problem | What is the fund asking, who is it about, why does care break down between visits, and why has the market not fixed it | Appendix A |
18	| 2. What the research found | What actually improves outcomes, how care has been scaled without specialists, what the technology can do, who else is doing this, where the money is, and what the rules say | Appendices B, C, D, E |
19	| 3. Analysis: what it all means | Where to play, how to win, which of the options to build and why | Appendix F |
20	| 4. The product we can build | What the home blood-pressure step loop is and how it works for the patient and the doctor | Appendix G |
21	| 5. The MVP | What gets built tonight, what can honestly be shown at noon, and what comes after | Appendix G |
22	| 6. Recommendation, risks and open questions | What to do, how to pitch it, its weak spots, and what the team still has to decide (the old part L) | Appendix H |
23	| 7. Method and limits | How this was made and how far to trust it (the old part M) | Appendix I |
24	
25	### Which part to read
26	
27	| If you are | Read |
28	|---|---|
29	| Anyone on the team, first time | Chapters 1 to 6, in order |
30	| Building the engine and screens | Chapters 4 and 5, then Appendix G, then Appendix C |
31	| Building the hardware | Chapter 5, then Appendix G (parts and the hardware test), then Appendix C (sensing and reading quality) |
32	| The biology student | Chapters 2.1 and 2.2, then Appendix B, then Appendix G (the protocol file and the test cases) |
33	| Leading the pitch | Chapters 1 to 6, then Appendix H (the mentor) and Appendix F (strategy and options) |
34	| Writing the one-page thesis | Appendix G (the draft), chapter 1 (the argument), Appendix A (the numbers) |
35	| Asked "who else is doing this" | Chapter 2.4, then Appendix D |
36	| Asked "how big is it" or "is it legal" | Chapters 2.5 and 2.6, then Appendix E |
37	
38	### How to trust a number here
39	
40	- **Every fact carries an ID that links to its source**, for example D1-01-F02. Appendix I is the register: what each research note recorded, the link, whether the page was opened or only seen in a search summary, and the verdict of the claims check where one was run. Numbers were read at source by one research agent; the load-bearing ones were then re-checked by a second.
41	- **"Search summary only"** marks a fact seen only in a search result, not on the page itself.
42	- **Some statements are ours, and marked so:** OUR VIEW (a judgement), OUR ARITHMETIC or OUR ESTIMATE (a sum or a guess from stated inputs), ASSUMPTION (an input we chose), OUR DESIGN (a design choice of ours), THEIR CLAIM (a company about itself), EXAMPLE (mock-up data). The option scores, the market model, the simulation and the price are all ours.
43	- **Mock-up screens show example data.** Every name and reading in them is invented.
44	- **What was not done:** no customer interviews; no measured split of public and private treatment; no current specialist counts; no Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps was found. Each appendix ends with what it could not find.
45	- **It is not medical or legal advice.** The legal sections say what the texts say and list the questions for a lawyer.
46	
47	**Contents**
48	
49	<!-- CONTENTS -->
50

1	## 4. The product we can build
2	
3	Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with how the same loop can carry other protocols.
4	
5	### 4.1 What it does
6	
7	OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who miss the 30-day review: the half who do not return (chapter 1). Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects it in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.
8	
9	The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then raise it to 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available), with a re-check after 30 days on each step. After the last step the sheet says: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." It covers adults over 30. Its safety rules are in section 4.7, and every protocol rule in this chapter comes from that sheet [D1-06-F14].
10	
11	### 4.2 The system map
12	
13	A loop that changes treatment has six stages. Open parts already exist for each (Appendix C); the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).
14	
15	| Stage | Its job | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| Sense | Get a number from the home | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
18	| Check | Was the reading taken properly | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
19	| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed step | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
20	| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
21	| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram chat plus a web form |
22	| Learn | Improve choices from each response | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |
23	
24	![System map of the step loop](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)
25	
26	*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*
27	
28	The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank, and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path (chapter 2.3 gives the reason); a model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.
29	
30	### 4.3 The patient side
31	
32	![Patient chat on the phone](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)
33	
34	*Mock-up with example data.*
35	
36	The patient uses a Telegram chat, or a web form if the chat fails, on a phone that may be a family member's (chapter 1). The chat prompts a measurement, takes a photo or a typed reading, asks two questions about tablets and delivers the change.
37	
38	The home-reading rule (OUR DESIGN, from published guidance): on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7, as the European Society of Hypertension advises; the same society says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use the same home line. So a mean at or above 135 systolic or 85 diastolic is "still high"; one session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".
39	
40	The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.
41	
42	The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; memory screens are rejected. General vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; the clip's time-stamped record (section 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built; Bluetooth only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].
43	
44	### 4.4 The doctor side
45	
46	![Clinician queue of proposal cards](adaptive-care-pictures/11-bp-doctor-queue.png)
47	
48	*Mock-up with example data.*
49	
50	The doctor sees a queue of cards, urgent ones first, batched once a day. Each card shows the current step, a 7-day sparkline (a small chart of the week's readings), the mean, the answer to the medicine question, the protocol line it quotes, the safety checks ticked and the proposed regimen, with Approve, Edit and Reject. A timer logs each decision. Because the card carries everything needed, the decision is one tap (OUR DESIGN).
51	
52	![One proposal card in detail](adaptive-care-pictures/12-bp-doctor-detail.png)
53	
54	*Mock-up with example data.*
55	
56	The approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name: OUR DESIGN, and a question for a lawyer, since the telemedicine guidelines want the registered doctor to deliver the prescription directly (chapter 2.6).
57	
58	### 4.5 Trusting the reading
59	
60	A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as an arm hanging at the side (chapter 2.3). ## 1. The problem

This chapter tells the problem as a story, before any answer. It starts with what the fund asked for and what that asks of a product. It then counts the people the challenge is about, follows them between clinic visits, listens to what they and their doctors say in public, and ends with why the market has not fixed the gap.

### 1.1 Who set the challenge and what it really asks

The challenge was set for SPARK Night (13-14 Nov 2026, Ashoka University) by Beyond Next Ventures, a fund that backs founders solving social issues with deep science and deep tech, and that works across Japan and India [D2-07-F8]. The event poster names as challenge mentor Karthik Varada, Senior Associate in the fund's India investment group, based in Bengaluru [D2-07-F1, D2-07-F2, D2-07-F3]. The fund's words:

> We need ways to manage chronic disease burden at scale despite limited access to resources, specialists and irregular clinical follow-ups. Patients need treatment methods that responds to their specific condition, and will remain adaptive to patient needs between appointments. How can digital therapeutics use rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers to continuously personalise care, thereby bringing measurable improvements in health outcomes to patients who cannot access frequent specialist support? The opportunity is to extend effective treatment into everyday life, beyond monitoring and reminders.

Read phrase by phrase, the challenge sets six requirements. The middle column is our reading; the right column says where this document gives the evidence.

| The fund's words | What a product must do (OUR VIEW) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| "rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers" | Use a signal that moves within days of a treatment change and is cheap and correct to measure at home. | Chapter 2.3 |
| "continuously personalise care" | Recompute the treatment from this patient's readings: the protocol step (a protocol is a written step-by-step treatment plan), the response to the last step, whether the medicine was taken, and what is unsafe. | Chapter 2.3 |
| "adaptive to patient needs between appointments" | Change the treatment without waiting for the next visit. | Chapter 1.3 |
| "measurable improvements in health outcomes" | Move one endpoint (the result a trial is judged on) within 90 days, past an accepted threshold for "clinically meaningful". | Chapter 2.1 |
| "patients who cannot access frequent specialist support" | Move the routine decision to a general doctor, nurse or health worker under a written protocol. The specialist owns the protocol and sees the exceptions. | Chapter 1.3 |
| "beyond monitoring and reminders" | Reach adaptive depth 4: the therapy itself changes. | Below, and chapter 2.1 |

#### What "beyond monitoring and reminders" rules in and out

This document sorts every product on an "adaptive depth" scale from 0 to 4: how far the product changes treatment. The fund names levels 1 and 2 and asks to go beyond them. OUR VIEW: it is asking for level 4.

| Level | What it means | Examples in the notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Uses no patient data | The Nerivio migraine wearable, switched on by the patient, rated 0-1 [D1-02-F12] |
| 1 | Shows data | Pocket ECGs in India (search summary only) [D1-04-F32]; Omron VitalSight abroad [D1-01-F39] |
| 2 | Sends reminders or generic content | India's government Simple app, with overdue lists and reminder messages [D3-05-F03]; the Medisafe reminder app abroad |
| 3 | Coaches from the person's own data | Sugar.fit, BeatO and Fitterfly in India [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]; CureApp HT in Japan |
| 4 | Changes the therapy: a dose, a protocol step, an exercise prescription | In India, only Sanofi's My Dose Coach was found, its Indian results unconfirmed [D1-04-F09]; abroad, d-Nav and insulin pumps [D1-05-F41] |

The line between 3 and 4 matters most. Level 3 changes the advice: what to eat, how to exercise. Level 4 changes the prescription: a new dose or a new protocol step. A clinician approving each change keeps a product at level 4. The test is simple: after the software runs, the prescription is different. OUR VIEW: level 4 is the entry condition, however good the sensor.

#### The loop: sense, decide, confirm, act, learn

A product at level 4 runs a loop of five stages. Monitoring products stop after the first.

- **Sense.** A home device gives a number, valid only if it was taken correctly. Level 1 products stop here.
- **Decide.** Software applies a written protocol to this patient's readings and proposes the next step. Coaching apps decide advice, not doses.
- **Confirm.** A doctor, nurse or health worker approves each change; unsafe cases go to a specialist.
- **Act.** The patient gets the new dose, medicine or exercise level.
- **Learn.** The next readings show whether it worked, and the loop runs again.

![The difference between monitoring and a therapy loop](adaptive-care-pictures/00-the-loop.png)

*Diagram: monitoring stops at the reading; a therapy loop sends the reading back as a changed treatment.*

OUR VIEW: the fund asks for a routine treatment decision between visits, from a home reading, by someone the patient can reach. The rest of this chapter shows who needs that decision and why it does not happen today.

### 1.2 Who it is about and how big it is

The challenge speaks of chronic disease "at scale". In India that scale is set first by high blood pressure and diabetes. The surveys measure different ages, use different blood-pressure rules and ran in different years, so they disagree; each figure is given with its source, and none is picked over the others.

| Condition | Figure | Year of data | Who was counted |
|---|---|---|---|
| High blood pressure | 35.5% | 2008-2020 | ICMR-INDIAB survey, adults 20+, blood pressure measured, 113,043 people in 31 states and union territories [D1-03-F01] |
| High blood pressure | 315 million people, a 2021 projection by the survey's investigators, not a count in the paper | Projected to 2021 | Same study [D1-03-F02] |
| High blood pressure | 22.6%; 24% of men, 21% of women (search summary only) | 2019-21 | NFHS-5 (National Family Health Survey), ages 15+ [D1-03-F03, D1-03-F04] |
| High blood pressure | 45.9% | 2017-19 | LASI (Longitudinal Ageing Study in India), adults 45+, 72,262 people [D1-03-F25] |
| Diabetes | 11.4%; prediabetes 15.3% | 2008-2020 | ICMR-INDIAB, adults 20+ [D1-03-F01] |
| Diabetes | 101 million; prediabetes 136 million, 2021 projections by the survey's investigators, not counts in the paper | Projected to 2021 | Same study [D1-03-F02] |
| Diabetes | 89.8 million (age-standardised 10.5%); 156.7 million projected for 2050 | 2024 | IDF Diabetes Atlas, adults 20-79 [D1-03-F28] |
| Heart failure | 1.3-4.6 million cases, or about 8-10 million (about 1% of the population; search summary only); no national survey | 2010; 2016 | Reviews built from local and disease-specific data [D3-07-F24, D3-07-F25] |

Why they differ, as the notes give it. For blood pressure, 35.5% and 22.6% come from different ages (20+ against 15+), years and use of the threshold [D1-03-F01, D1-03-F04], and LASI counts only people aged 45 and over. For diabetes, the 101 million is a 2021 projection of survey rates on a different survey base and age definition from the 89.8 million [D1-03-F02, D1-03-F28].

Other long-term conditions are large too. COPD (chronic lung disease) and asthma had 55.3 million and 37.9 million cases in 2016 (search summary only) [D1-03-F36]. The Global Burden of Disease study put India's stroke cases at 9.4 million in 2021, up from 4.4 million in 1990 (press report quoting the authors) [D3-07-F26]. Heart failure has no national count, but its registries show a treatment gap: in the National Heart Failure Registry (10,851 acute patients, 53 hospitals, 21 states), 47.5% of eligible patients received guideline drugs, and 1-year death was 22.1% [D1-01-F47, D1-01-F48].

OUR VIEW: on any count, blood pressure is the largest pool.

#### Knowing, treated, controlled

A care cascade follows people with a condition through four steps: has it, knows it, is treated, is controlled. India's government hypertension programme, the India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI), surveyed the same nine districts twice, with no comparison districts.

![Share of adults with high blood pressure who know, are treated and are controlled, 2018-19 and 2023-24](adaptive-care-pictures/22-india-cascade.png)

*Chart: in the first nine districts of India's hypertension programme, 21.2% of adults with high blood pressure were under control in 2023-24, up from 14.5% in 2018-19 [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11].*

In the same surveys, awareness rose from 52.4% to 58.5% and treatment from 40.8% to 44.7%, among 7,047 and then 7,324 people with hypertension [D1-01-F10, D1-03-F12]. In two districts control was under 5% at the start [D1-01-F10]. Nationally, a preprint on the 2019-21 family health survey (1.69 million adults) counts 36.7% of all people with hypertension as aware, 17.7% as treated and 9.1% (about 1 in 11) as controlled [D1-03-F07]. Counted only among people aged 15-49 who are already on drugs, the same survey gives 73.7% controlled [D1-03-F06]; the ages and the denominators (the group a percentage is taken of) differ, so the two figures do not compare. For diabetes, 43% of cases, about 38.6 million, were undiagnosed in 2024 [D1-03-F28].

#### Treatment is not control

Getting people onto medicine is not enough. Tamil Nadu's doorstep programme, Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, was surveyed in 6,856 adults aged 30 and over across all 38 districts (paper abstract, 2025; a news report gives 6,809). Screening reached 79.4% for diabetes and 82.6% for hypertension, and over 95% of diagnosed people were on treatment. Yet control rates were 9.8% for diabetes and 35.4% for hypertension; the abstract does not say whether these are shares of everyone with the disease, of the diagnosed or of the treated [D1-03-F09].

OUR VIEW: two steps leak, diagnosis and control. The step from "treated" to "controlled" depends on the dose being raised and the medicine being taken.

#### The world and Japan

Low control is a world problem. About 1.4 billion people aged 30-79 have hypertension; 44% do not know it, 23% are controlled, and two-thirds live in low- and middle-income countries (2024) [D1-03-F32]. There are 830 million adults with diabetes, and 59% of those aged 30 and over are not on diabetes medicine (2022) [D1-03-F33]. Japan, the fund's home, has about 43 million people with hypertension, about 31 million (73%) of them poorly controlled (2010 base, cited for 2017; search summary only) [D1-03-F47], and 29.4% of its people were aged 65 or over in September 2025 (search summary only) [D1-03-F48]. OUR VIEW: "treated but not controlled" is the gap in Japan too, so the problem is not only Indian.

### 1.3 Why care breaks down between visits

India does not lack programmes. It screens and treats on a scale few countries match. The breakdown comes after the first prescription, in the weeks between visits.

#### A large system that sees people once

| Programme | Scale (date) |
|---|---|
| National NCD (non-communicable disease) screening | 41.5 crore people screened for hypertension and 41.3 crore for diabetes (cumulative, Aug 2026) [D1-03-F20] |
| "75 by 25" (75 million on standard care by 2025) | 42.01 million hypertension patients put on standard care by the public programme as of 5 Mar 2025, and 25.27 million diabetes patients (search summary only; three outlets agree) [D1-03-F14] |
| Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (12 free services) | Over 1.86 lakh functional (Aug 2026) [D1-03-F19] |
| NCD clinics | 770 district clinics and 6,410 at community health centres (2026) [D1-03-F20] |
| eSanjeevani teleconsultation | Over 49 crore consultations by Aug 2026 [D1-03-F19] |
| Jan Aushadhi Kendras (generic medicine shops) | 18,646 (Feb 2026), priced 50-80% below branded medicines [D1-03-F20] |

#### The return visit that half never make

IHCI runs a fixed drug protocol. Its cohort registered 21,895 patients at 24 sites in Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Telangana (Jan 2018-Jun 2019) and followed them up in Jul-Sep 2019, with no comparison group. Only 11,274 (51%) came back. Among those who did, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% [D1-03-F10]. A second cohort, 281,209 patients started in Punjab and Maharashtra in 2018-2021, found 36% with no visit in Jan-Mar 2022; the two cohorts differ in sites, years and the definition of loss [D3-05-F04]. Another count found about 27% of registered IHCI patients did not return in Jan-Mar 2021 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13].

The visit matters because the dose waits for it. A doctor dispenses the first medicine. Trained paramedical staff dispense the monthly refill only when pressure is controlled; uncontrolled patients are sent to a doctor for a dose change [D3-05-F08]. A patient who does not go back stays on the same dose. Some also stop taking it: pooled Indian non-adherence (adherence means taking the medicine as prescribed) to blood-pressure drugs is 48%, with a prediction interval of 9-90% (search summary only) [D1-03-F44].

#### Few specialists, two minutes

In March 2023, 79.9% of the required posts in four specialities (surgeon, physician, paediatrician, obstetrician-gynaecologist) at rural community health centres were unfilled [D1-03-F16], and the shortfall has stayed near 17,500 posts since 2014-15 [D1-03-F17]. The only specialist counts are from a 2017 parliamentary committee (search summary only): about 4,000 cardiologists, 1,200 nephrologists and 650 endocrinologists, against the committee's estimated needs of 88,000, 40,000 and 28,000 [D1-03-F18]. The government told Parliament it does not hold speciality-wise doctor data (news report of the reply, 13 Apr 2025) [D3-07-F22]. Where patients do see a doctor, the visit is short: Indian primary-care visits lasted about 2.3 minutes (2013, stopwatch, 412 visits) and 2 minutes (2015), against 10.2 minutes in Japan (2012) [D1-03-F24].

#### Cost

Families pay a large share of the bill. Out-of-pocket spending was 39.4% of total health expenditure in 2021-22 and 43.41% in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts released 27 May 2026, via a news report); in 2022-23 household spending rose by ₹26,375 crore while government spending fell by nearly ₹49,000 crore [D1-03-F23]. The notes found no figure for the household cost of a chronic-care visit, travel distance or lost wages, the share of chronic patients who see a doctor each year, loss to follow-up outside IHCI, or how many months a dose change is delayed.

#### Phones and who is left out

Most Indians have a mobile connection, but the patient is not always the one who holds it.

| Measure | Figure | Year |
|---|---|---|
| Smartphone owners | Over 622 million (industry estimate) [D1-03-F41] | 2025 |
| Women 15-49 owning a phone | 63.6%; rural 57.4% (search summary only) [D1-03-F42] | 2023-24 |
| Women 15-49 owning the phone they use (another note) | 54%; rural 46.6% [D3-04-F23] | Not stated |
| Phone ownership, ages 15+ | Men 83.9%, women 56.2% (search summary only) [D1-03-F42] | 2025 |
| Rural older adults near Mysore (150 people) | 50% owned a phone, few a smartphone; digital literacy 11% [D3-04-F56] | Not stated |
| People who spoke English | About 10.6% [D3-04-F57] | 2011 |

About four in ten rural women do not own a phone (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 57.4 = 42.6%). OUR VIEW: anything that reaches patients between visits must work on a shared phone, through a health worker, and by voice.

OUR VIEW: a two-minute visit has no time to read two weeks of home readings, and the visit itself is the step that about half the patients skip.

### 1.4 What patients and doctors say in public

The numbers show where care breaks. The voices show why. The team has done no interviews, so this section reports published interview studies and surveys (PUBLISHED STUDY), public app reviews (PUBLIC REVIEW) and posts (FORUM POST). None of it is customer evidence gathered by the team; reviews are self-selected, and the studies were read as abstracts only.

#### Why patients miss follow-up and stop medicines

Eight Indian interview studies (PUBLISHED STUDY) name the same causes: feeling well, cost, family duties, fear of long-term drugs and traditional medicine [D3-04-F01, D3-04-F02, D3-04-F03, D3-04-F04, D3-04-F05, D3-04-F12, D3-04-F13, D3-04-F14]. In coastal Karnataka, 32 patients lost to follow-up described "symptom-driven healthcare seeking", work duties, wage loss and rushed consultations, and suggested reminders and digital records [D3-04-F01]. In rural Tamil Nadu, stopping was structural, unintentional (work, travel, caregiving) or intentional, and family could both help and hinder [D3-04-F02]. In Ludhiana, "about 50% patients were adherent" among 40 people with diabetes [D3-04-F14]. In Chennai, caregivers enable access for older adults and devices are shared [D3-04-F05]. A FORUM POST by an adult child says the father's pressure stayed controlled on Ayurvedic treatment, then rose, and he went back to some medication [D3-04-F52].

One small survey puts numbers on it. In Bathinda (Punjab), 157 people who had missed visits for over 3 months were phoned (a small convenience sample): 24.8% had no sense of being ill, 22.2% named distance, 15.2% had no guidance or reminder and 8.2% had an acute illness [D3-05-F07].

OUR VIEW: feeling well recurs as a reason to stop, and a home reading is one thing that can contradict it.

#### Home monitors in Indian homes

Few patients use a home cuff, most taught themselves, and home readings show that many "controlled" patients are not.

- **Who has one.** Of 2,588 clinic-attending people with hypertension and caregivers in North India, 18.1% used a home monitor (urban 20.5%, rural 8.5%); 75.2% learned by themselves, and technique was excellent in 15.9% of patients and 5.9% of caregivers [D3-04-F06]. No household survey figure was found. Omron says household penetration is "below 5%" (2026 article) or "just 2%" (2024 article) (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-07-F14, D3-07-F15]; another report gives 6% (search summary only) [D2-05-F29]; a web claim of under 5% cites no source [D3-04-F22].
- **What doctors do with them.** About 88% of 832 Indian doctors recommend home monitoring but estimate that only 30.4% of patients measure, and about 30% give no instructions [D3-04-F07]. Only 15.1% knew the correct home thresholds [D3-04-F18].
- **What home readings reveal.** In the GRAND study (18 centres, 12 states, 1,920 treated patients who attend regularly, 7 days of home readings), 77.7% looked controlled by clinic pressure but only 55.9% by clinic plus home; 21.8% had masked uncontrolled pressure (high at home, normal in clinic) [D3-04-F09].

#### What doctors and health workers say

Doctors describe heavy workloads, and many private doctors do not follow the state protocol. In Kolar, Karnataka: "Doctors face very high workloads, especially in the public sector" [D3-04-F16]. Of 30 private doctors in Bhopal, 19 did not follow the state protocol, citing fear of losing patients if pressure did not come down at once, or of causing drug side effects, and a preference for fixed-dose combinations (two drugs in one tablet) [D3-04-F15]. Two people who run programmes wrote on LinkedIn (paraphrased; numbers in their posts are unverified; read 13 Nov 2026). A national NCD consultant at UNICEF India (about Apr 2026) said programmes failed on blood-pressure machines left uncalibrated for months and on mid-month drug stock-outs. A doctor and WHO consultant (about Oct 2026) said counting visits is not enough, and cited an Indian trial, mWellcare (chapter 2.1), as showing that a digital system does not guarantee results. No Indian doctor, nurse or health worker was found speaking about dose steps from home readings. OUR VIEW: a doctor's approval cannot be assumed.

#### What users say about existing programmes

The latest 100 Apple App Store India reviews of each of three diabetes programmes, BeatO, Sugar.fit and Fitterfly, were read on 13 Nov 2026. One-star reviews numbered 55, 76 and 9 (count from the research note's method section); Fitterfly's 5-star profile looks prompted (the note's inference). The complaints fall into a few themes (PUBLIC REVIEW).

| Theme | What reviewers describe |
|---|---|
| Unwanted calls | Repeated recorded calls and WhatsApp messages about classes and webinars the reviewer never signed up for (Sugar.fit, Jul and Oct 2026) [D3-04-F27, D3-04-F28] |
| No reachable person | No doctor slot for days; no support line that answers (Sugar.fit, Sep and Oct 2026) [D3-04-F29, D3-04-F30] |
| Coaching runs dry | "by the third month, there is hardly anything new to discuss" (Sugar.fit, 26 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F33]; no follow-up after a month [D3-04-F34] |
| Device and data | A sensor whose data never synced; five readings in five minutes that differed by over 50 (BeatO, Sep and Mar 2026) [D3-04-F36, D3-04-F37] |
| Money and medicine | ₹18,990 paid for a 4-month programme with, the reviewer says, only one month's medicine delivered; a refund still pending after about 20 days (Sugar.fit, Oct 2026; BeatO, Jul 2026) [D3-04-F40, D3-04-F42] |
| Praise for a named coach | Credit to a personal coach; one reviewer reports HbA1c (a blood test of average sugar over about three months) down to 6.1 and medicine halved (Fitterfly, 2025 and 2024) [D3-04-F43, D3-04-F44] |

None of the 300 reviews mentions language or voice, and none describes a dose change from a home reading (count from the research note's method section).

#### Reminders and messages

Reminders alone did not bring people back. In a Punjab trial at two public hospitals, 388 patients with uncontrolled pressure got two myth-busting WhatsApp reminders before their visit, or none; attendance was 21.8% against 19.6%, a null result, and beliefs did not change [D3-04-F50]. A Delhi study of 110 patients (counselling, voice calls, SMS) reported control rising from 14.7% to 52.9%, but with no control group [D3-04-F51].

OUR VIEW: patients stop when they feel well, few use a cuff well, doctors are stretched and wary of the protocol, and a message works only if it reaches the person who holds the phone and leads to a decision.

### 1.5 The market issues: why the market has not fixed this

The gap is clear, so the next thing to explain is why companies have not filled it. Three answers recur in the notes: what has been sold stops before the dose, the companies that sold apps on their own ran out of money, and nobody yet pays for the step that is missing.

#### What has been sold so far

India's private chronic-care programmes sell a glucose sensor or meter plus a doctor and a coach. None of their pages says glucose data changes a drug dose by algorithm, so on what is published they sit at adaptive depth 3 [D1-04-F02, D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. Their outcome figures are their own averages with no comparison group (THEIR CLAIM) [D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. The patient pays: Sugar.fit charges ₹29,990 for 12 months or ₹15,990 for 4 months (13 Nov 2026) [D1-04-F04], and HealthifyRx charged ₹48,000 for 3 months (May 2025) [D1-04-F26].

The government's tools stop at the same place. IHCI runs a fixed state drug-and-dose protocol, and its Simple app keeps a registry, flags overdue patients and sends reminders [D1-04-F19]. The app's protocol model stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step logic was found in it [D1-06-F40]. So the nurse records the reading, but the step-up decision still waits for a visit.

#### Why companies died

Abroad, several companies sold digital therapeutics (software that changes one patient's treatment) or sensors, some with good trials, and failed. India's best-funded chronic-care app did too.

| Company | What it sold | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Pear Therapeutics (US) | Prescription apps for addiction and insomnia, with randomised trials [D1-02-F17] | Bankrupt April 2023; assets sold for just over $6M against $130M of liabilities [D1-05-F20, D1-02-F42]. A panel said it tried to change care and payment at once [D1-05-F21] |
| Akili (US) | A game for ADHD in children | $523,000 of prescription revenue in 2023, net loss $59.5M; sale agreed for about $34M in May 2024 [D1-02-F44] |
| Better Therapeutics (US) | A diabetes app: HbA1c 0.39 points lower than a control app (669 patients, 90 days) [D1-02-F21] | Expected no revenue in 2023 (revenue not reported), deficit $134.3M; weighed winding down in March 2024 [D1-02-F46] |
| Teva Digihaler | Sensor inhalers and app | US distribution and app support stopped 1 June 2024; the US notice gave no reason and a UK recall cited "commercial reasons" [D1-02-F41] |
| Babylon | Digital primary care | Lost NHS contracts; $221M loss on about $1B revenue; UK business sold for just over $600,000 in 2023 [D1-05-F54] |
| PhableCare (India) | Blood-pressure and glucose devices, consultations (depth 2) | Raised ₹187 crore in Apr 2022; stopped work in Feb 2023; staff fell from about 2,000 to 200, many unpaid. Former staff said there were no funds; the founders blamed staff misconduct [D1-04-F14, D1-04-F23] |

The common causes, as the notes give them:

- No one paid for the app alone [D1-05-F20, D1-02-F44, D1-05-F23].
- Too few prescribers, and trials that payers did not accept as outcome proof [D1-05-F21].
- Sensors with no therapy change [D1-02-F41, D1-02-F02].
- Valuations ahead of revenue, then no cash [D1-05-F55, D1-04-F23].
- Users leave fast: across 93 mental-health apps, the median app kept 3.3% of its users at day 30 [D1-02-F26].

#### Who pays today

In India, the patient pays for private programmes, as above, and the state pays for public care, where treatment "could be as low as Rs 200 per patient per year", a modelled drug cost that leaves out staff (WHO, 2022; SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D2-01-F12, D2-05-F18, D3-05-F09]. The notes found no Indian payer, public or private, that pays for remote blood-pressure monitoring or a digital therapeutic as a line item [D2-04-F47]. Insurance barely touches outpatient care: outpatient cover is below 0.1% of a US$37.7 billion outpatient market (industry-sponsored, search summary only) [D2-05-F10].

Abroad, the firms that reached scale are paid by someone other than the patient. Employers and insurers pay for clinician-led programmes: Hinge Health, paid "primarily" by employers, earned $234.97M in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16]. Or the company sells a device that delivers the therapy: Insulet, a closed-loop insulin pump maker, earned $842.0M in the same quarter [D1-05-F41].

#### No dose change found

No Indian service was found that turns home blood-pressure or glucose readings into a medicine change between visits [D1-04-F09, D1-04-F19]. This was one agent's limited search on 13 Nov 2026, a search result and not proof of absence; chapter 2.4 lists the searches and the nearest products abroad.

OUR VIEW: India's best-funded chronic-care app ran out of money within a year of its largest round. Money raised is not proof that anyone will pay, and a product sold to the patient alone has, so far, not lasted.

### 1.6 The problem in one paragraph

OUR VIEW. Hundreds of millions of Indians have high blood pressure or diabetes, many are on medicine, and few are controlled. India already screens and enrols them at crore scale, and its programme has a protocol and free drugs. What it lacks between visits is the decision, the confirmation and the action. The scarce thing is the prescriber's decision, which waits for a visit that about half the patients do not make, and when they do come, the visit lasts about two minutes. The products sold so far show readings, send reminders or coach, and stop before the dose; the companies that sold an app on its own died, because nobody paid for it.

Full detail: Appendix A (the challenge, the burden and the voices), with Appendix D for the companies and Appendix E for who pays.

The problem is now clear: a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that watches and reminds but does not change the treatment. The next chapter asks what the research says actually works, and whether anyone has made it work without specialists.
