- **SOM.** Clinics live and paying patients per clinic at each year end, after an unpaid pilot year (all ASSUMPTION): 15 clinics in year 2, 60 in year 3, 180 in year 4 and 400 in year 5.

The unused counts rest on the 2021 projection of adults with high blood pressure (chapter 1.2) times the 17.7% treated share from a preprint (chapter 1.2), and on assumed shares of 13,88,185 registered doctors (reply to Parliament, December 2025) [D2-05-F38]. The weakest inputs are the 50% and 20% shares, which are guesses; the 50% is in line with smartphone access figures for older adults (chapter 3.2) [D3-07-F11]. The model leaves out public-system patients, diabetes and other conditions, device sales and every country outside India.

#### The US$100 million-a-year test

US$100 million a year is ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026). At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients (52,71,253). The serviceable market holds 41.9 lakh. **On this model the test fails in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (all OUR ARITHMETIC). At higher prices fewer patients are needed: 7,85,417 at ₹1,000 a month, 3,92,708 at ₹2,000, and 3,40,136 at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month [D2-05-F23]. The rest would have to come from more protocols on the same loop, a paid public tier, other countries that use the same family of protocols, or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.

| Price a month (ASSUMPTION) | SAM used | SOM year 5 (bottom-up) | Patients needed for US$100 million |
|---|---|---|---|
| ₹99 | ₹498 crore | ₹11.9 crore | 79.3 lakh |
| ₹149 | ₹749 crore | ₹17.9 crore | 52.7 lakh |
| ₹299 | ₹1,504 crore | ₹35.9 crore | 26.3 lakh |

A public tier, shown apart: 420.1 lakh patients on treatment in the public programme [D1-03-F14] x ₹15 a month (ASSUMPTION) x 12 = ₹756 crore a year (OUR ARITHMETIC). A state would pay this only for results.

OUR VIEW: blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company. Price moves the result as much as clinic count does.

#### Unit economics, per patient a month

Every cost line is an ASSUMPTION from the build note, to be checked.

| Line | Value |
|---|---|
| Price to the clinic, private tier | ₹149 per active patient (ASSUMPTION), below Sugar.fit's ₹2,499 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹29,990 / 12) |
| Messages | ₹15 (WhatsApp templates; Telegram costs nothing). Two resellers copying Meta's India card give ₹0.115 a utility message and ₹0.8631 a marketing message, before 18% GST, from 1 Oct 2026 (third party, not Meta) [D3-07-F20, D3-07-F21] |
| Cloud and storage | ₹5 |
| Reading cuff photos | ₹2 (about 30 photos) |
| Health-worker call to silent patients | ₹30 (one 5-minute call a month) |
| Doctor time | 6.5-8.5 proposals per 100 patients a month at 30 seconds each, about 4 minutes per 100 patients; not costed (OUR SIMULATION and ASSUMPTION) |
| **Gross margin** | **₹149 - (15 + 5 + 2 + 30) = ₹97, about 65% (OUR ARITHMETIC)** |

OUR VIEW: the health-worker call is the largest cost, and the margin holds only if doctors approve proposals without being paid per approval.

#### What comparable companies earn and are worth

| Company | Revenue and result | Funding, value or exit |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar.fit (India) | FY25 ₹66.5 crore (+77%), loss ₹42 crore [D2-05-F19] | Not in these notes |
| Healthify (India) | FY23 ₹228.76 crore, loss ₹142 crore; FY24 about ₹206.3 crore, loss about ₹88 crore (aggregators) [D2-05-F22] | US$20M Series D, Oct 2024 |
| Omada (US) | Revenue per member US$294 a year, about US$24.5 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: 294 / 12); gross margin 76%; net income US$6.551M in Q3 2026 [D2-05-F23, D1-05-F12] | Listed |
| Twin Health (US) | Revenue NOT FOUND | US$53M Series E at about US$950M (Aug 2025) [D2-05-F15, D1-05-F48] |

No US medicine-adjusting programme publishes a price per member a month. On cost-effectiveness, a 35-year model of TASMINH2 (UK, self-titration against usual care, 2014) gave about £1,624 per QALY (a year of life in full health) for men and £4,923 for women, if the blood-pressure gain lasts 2 years for men and 5 for women (SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D2-05-F25]; no Indian study was found.

The funding climate is warm abroad and thin in Indian health. US digital health raised US$7.4 billion in 244 deals in H1 2026, against US$6.4 billion in H1 2025, with deals of US$100 million or more taking 45% [D2-05-F16]. Indian health-tech raised US$310 million in H1 2026 (headline only, tracker not named) [D2-05-F11], out of US$7.2 billion for all Indian tech start-ups (search summary only) [D2-05-F13].

OUR VIEW: about US$24.5 of revenue a member a month is reached abroad only with employer and insurer payers. Indian comparables are small, loss-making and sold at undisclosed prices.

### 2.6 The rules

> **In short.**
> - India's July 2026 guidance treats software that guides treatment as a medical device; a doctor-approved dose proposal could fall in Class A, B or C, which the regulator confirms.
> - In telemedicine, only a registered doctor may prescribe, and must deliver the prescription directly.
> - A study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first.
> - Abroad, each country pays through a clinician, and Germany ties part of the price to results.

These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO, India's medical-device regulator.

#### Software as a medical device

CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. India has four risk classes, A lowest and D highest, and the class follows the intended use, as stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. Its grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:

| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | D | C | B |
| Serious | C | B | A |
| Non-serious | B | A | A |

"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal that a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", and Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits [D2-04-F05], and a patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical". CDSCO names a hypertension digital-therapeutics platform and a Bluetooth cuff app as medical device software, and bars the wellness carve-out once a disease is named [D2-04-F07, D2-04-F09]. Unlike the US, India has no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. OUR VIEW: clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.

#### Testing on patients

A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14], which the flowchart says is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. Whether a pilot in which software drafts and a doctor decides counts as a clinical investigation is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Trials must be registered on CTRI before the first patient, with ethics approval uploaded (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]. Fees and processing days were NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].

#### Who may prescribe and change a dose

The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; such tools may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. A follow-up, under the same guidelines, means the same doctor and the same condition within 6 months of the last in-person consultation [D2-04-F17, D2-01-F10]. Whether later rules changed this in 2026 was not checked. In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription", and no law, rule or ministry order was found that lets a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18].

The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats conditions in its Schedule, which lists "Diabetes", "Heart diseases" and "High or low blood pressure"; whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested [D2-04-F31].

#### What tonight's prototype may and may not say

OUR VIEW, drawn from the rules above:
- It is a prototype for test and demonstration, not a medical device on sale and not tested on patients.
- It uses open data, simulated patients or teammates' readings, and no patient data.
- A clinician approves every dose change and directly delivers the prescription; the software only drafts and shows its reasons.
- It makes no claim that it treats or controls high blood pressure, and no claim of benefit to patients.

#### Rules and payment abroad

| Country | Device rule | How it is paid |
|---|---|---|
| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k), for example My Dose Coach and d-Nav [D2-04-F24]. Software that supports a clinician who can review its basis, and does not analyse a device signal, is not a device; whether home cuff readings count as a signal is a question for counsel [D2-04-F22, D2-04-F23] | Medicare remote monitoring needs a face-to-face initiating visit from 1 Jan 2027 [D2-04-F26] |
| Germany | The DiGA route requires a positive care effect, with a decision in 3 months [D2-04-F28] | Price negotiated after year one; from 1 Jan 2026 at least 20% of the price must depend on measured outcomes [D2-04-F29, D1-05-F31] |
| Japan | CureApp HT, approved in April 2022, has been insured since 1 Sep 2022 as an add-on app that coaches lifestyle (salt, weight, exercise), not a dose change [D3-06-F19, D2-04-F37] | From 1 Jun 2026, 90 points a month in person or 78 online, plus 7,010 yen for the app (company release and a news report); the patient pays 30% (search summary only) [D2-04-F43, D3-06-F20]. Older figures differ: 7,010 yen (Jan 2024) or about 2,490 yen a month at a 30% patient share (2022), on different bases, unreconciled [D1-05-F33]; about 8,000 yen (search summary only) [D1-01-F57] |

OUR VIEW: all three pay through a clinician, and Germany now ties part of the price to outcomes.

Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player) and Appendix E (money and rules).

OUR VIEW: the research points one way. The treatment change, made by someone allowed to make it, is what works; India's programme has everything for it except a decision between visits; the technology to trust a home reading and bound a decision exists in open parts; nobody in India sells it; and nobody yet pays for it. The next chapter puts these findings together and weighs what to build.

## 2. What the research found

Chapter 1 showed a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that stops before the dose. This chapter condenses what the research found, in plain words. It starts with the clinical evidence on what actually improves outcomes, then turns to how others have scaled care without specialists, what the technology can and cannot do, who is already doing this, where the money is and what the rules allow.

### 2.1 What actually improves outcomes

> **In short.**
> - Outcomes improved when a home reading led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when the reading was only shown or turned into a reminder.
> - Who was allowed to change the dose mattered more than the electronics.
> - Raising adherence on its own did not move outcomes.
> - The same pattern holds in diabetes, heart failure, warfarin and asthma, and the known harms of dose stepping can be met with stop rules.

The trials sort into five rules. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.

#### Rule 1. The reading must change the treatment

Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring of blood pressure alone lowered systolic pressure (the upper number, in mmHg, millimetres of mercury) by 1.0 mmHg against usual care: no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, it fell 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05].

Where the dose itself moved, the falls were larger. In TASMIN-SR (UK, 59 practices, 552 patients at high cardiovascular risk, randomised: people got each treatment by chance), patients stepping their own dose by an agreed plan had systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg lower than under usual care at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. In HyperLink (US, 16 primary-care clinics randomised as clusters, meaning whole clinics rather than single patients, 450 patients), pharmacists adjusted drugs from home readings for 12 months and got 57.2% of patients controlled against 30.0% with usual care [D1-01-F04]. An independent US review by the Peterson Health Technology Institute (PHTI, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful" and programmes where virtual care teams adjust drugs "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg fall in systolic pressure [D1-01-F39]. The same split appears in warfarin and heart failure (table below).

![Extra fall in systolic pressure against usual care, by what was done with the reading](adaptive-care-pictures/20-what-lowers-pressure.png)

*Chart: separate trials with different patients and end points, so compare the groups, not single bars [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F05, D1-01-F06, D1-01-F07].*

#### Rule 2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics

In TASMINH4 (UK, 142 practices, 1,182 patients, 12 months), the family doctor adjusted doses in every arm; sending home readings electronically instead of on paper added 1.2 mmHg, not significant (small enough to be chance) [D1-01-F03]. In rural China, the China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP: 326 villages, 33,995 people aged 40 and over) let village doctors start and step drugs by a standard protocol, supervised by primary-care physicians. At 18 months, 57.0% were under 130/80 against 19.9% with enhanced usual care, with no treatment-related serious adverse events [D1-01-F09]. After a median of 4 years, cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, heart-failure admission, cardiovascular death) were lower, with a hazard ratio (a risk ratio measured over time; below 1 means fewer events) of 0.75 at age 60 and over and 0.64 under 60. The caveat matters: the programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates, so the effect cannot be credited to the protocol alone [D1-01-F38].

India has the null result that belongs here. mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps during visits. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67), not significant; both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run protocol programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail, because the app did not act on home readings or reach patients who never came back, and no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a dose protocol was found (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).

![Share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose](adaptive-care-pictures/21-share-controlled.png)

*Chart: three settings where someone other than a specialist was allowed to step the dose. The China programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results; the India figures are before and after among the 51% who returned, with no comparison group [D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09, D1-03-F10].*

#### Rule 3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes

Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (ASCENT, 23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children raised adherence to 84% against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. A blood-pressure reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 US adults, 12 weeks) moved systolic pressure by 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.

#### Rule 4. Someone must pay for the outcome

Chapter 1.5 told this side: apps and sensors sold on their own failed, while the firms that lasted are paid by employers and insurers for clinician-led programmes, or sell a device that delivers the therapy.

#### Rule 5. People stay when their own clinician is in it

In eight remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants), median retention was 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, and payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27]. In trials of chronic-disease apps, pooled dropout was 43% [D1-02-F28]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.

#### What the loop changes, by kind

The same pattern shows when therapies are sorted by what the feedback loop changes.

| What the loop changes | Home signal | How fast it responds | Proof | Who decides |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (a blood test of clotting time), weight | Days to weeks: insulin every 3 days in a 2025 US rule [D1-06-F16]; blood pressure re-checked at 30 days [D1-06-F14] | Strong: randomised trials with fewer deaths, clots or hospital stays | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker |
| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Each meal [D1-01-F22] | Mixed | App, coach |
| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Each session [D1-06-F36] | Matches in-person care; no better than usual care | Therapist or app |
| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Automatic | Strong | Algorithm, within limits a clinician sets [D1-05-F41] |
| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | During practice [D1-02-F15] | Weak | Patient |

OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none.

#### The evidence by condition

| Condition | What works | How strong | Main caution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blood pressure | Dose stepping from home readings by the patient, a pharmacist or a village doctor (rules 1 and 2) | Strongest: randomised trials up to hard outcomes at 4 years | Leg swelling 32% against 22% with patient self-titration in TASMINH2 [D1-01-F01]; the China gain came with free drugs and incentives |
| Type 2 diabetes | Software that computes the insulin dose. d-Nav (181 adults on insulin, 3 US centres, 6 months, device plus clinician support against clinician support alone): HbA1c down 1.0 point against 0.3, low blood sugar 0.29 against 0.29 events a month [D1-01-F13]. With a glucose sensor in both arms, an automated dose algorithm cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points (2IQP, 319 adults, US and Canada, 13 weeks, funded by the pump maker) [D1-01-F43] | Good; d-Nav was funded by the US NIH, but several authors were maker staff or shareholders | Low blood sugar. PHTI (March 2024) found US type 2 tools without a continuous glucose monitor "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits" [D1-01-F40]. The large nutrition effects come from company-linked or non-randomised studies [D1-01-F19, D1-01-F21] |
| Heart failure | Fast dose stepping after discharge. STRONG-HF (87 hospitals, 14 countries, 1,078 patients, against usual care): readmission or death at 180 days an adjusted 15.2% against 23.3% [D1-01-F27] | Strong; stopped early for benefit; funded by Roche Diagnostics, a maker of heart-strain blood tests | More side effects (41% against 29%), four clinic visits in two months, lab tests. Telemonitoring without a mandated dose protocol was null in two US trials of 1,653 and 1,437 patients [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33] |
| Warfarin (a blood thinner) | Patients who test INR at home and set their own dose by a schedule: clots risk ratio (risk with treatment divided by risk without) 0.47, deaths 0.55, against usual care. Those who tested at home and left the dose to the clinic had no fewer deaths (0.94) [D1-02-F05] | Strong: 28 trials, 8,950 patients | The two approaches were compared with usual care in separate sets of trials, not with each other |
| Asthma | One inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose (SMART): flare-ups risk ratio 0.68 (16 trials, 22,748 people aged 12 and over) [D1-02-F37] | Strong, and no sensor is needed | A sensor inhaler system's benefit was uncertain: its interval crossed 1 (odds ratio for control 1.35) [D1-02-F02] |
| Gout | Nurses stepping urate-lowering drugs to a target: 95% reached it against 30% under GP care (517 patients, UK, 2 years) [D1-02-F06] | One trial | Not digital: a protocol run by nurses |
| Rehabilitation | Tele-rehabilitation matched centre rehabilitation in lung disease [D1-02-F03]; after stroke it was about equal to in-person physiotherapy and no better than usual care for daily activities (661 people) [D1-02-F07] | Matches in-person care | App-only exercise is "unlikely to be effective as total substitutes" (PHTI, June 2024) [D1-02-F54] |
| Guided breathing (biofeedback) | Systolic 3.67 mmHg lower across 8 trials [D1-02-F11] | Weak | No effect once the 5 maker-linked trials were removed |

#### Prescription apps and safety

Software sold as a prescribed treatment has passed trials, yet most of the companies behind it failed (chapter 1.5). The research note records that none of the prescription apps it lists changes a drug dose; most deliver scripted therapy content at adaptive depth 2-3. The closest to this topic is Japan's CureApp HT, a lifestyle-coaching app with no drug change: in 390 untreated adults with hypertension (12 sites, open-label, 12 weeks) it lowered 24-hour systolic pressure 2.4 mmHg more than lifestyle advice alone [D1-01-F07]. OUR VIEW: that is about half the effect of the dose-stepping trials, in patients not yet on drugs.

OUR VIEW: dose stepping by protocol has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. At 4 years in rural China, injurious falls, symptomatic low blood pressure, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups [D1-01-F38], and insulin-dose proposals in TeleDiab-2 (191 adults starting long-acting insulin, 4 months) caused no severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The known costs are more minor side effects, leg swelling in self-managed blood-pressure care and low blood sugar with insulin, so each needs its own safety branch.

### 2.2 How care has been scaled without specialists

> **In short.**
> - India's programme already has a protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list; the dose step still waits for a doctor's visit.
> - Patients who keep attending do well on the protocol; the loss is among those who stop coming.
> - Abroad, the largest gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill.
> - Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.

Chapter 2.1 showed that changing the dose works. This section asks how that has been delivered at scale without specialists, in India and abroad.

#### India's hypertension programme in practice

IHCI's design has three parts. A state protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first, with a review every 30 days (chapter 4.1 gives one state's steps); Punjab and Maharashtra order the steps differently at the second step [D3-05-F01, D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]. Free drugs, given as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres to district hospitals [D3-05-F02]. And the open-source Simple app, which takes about 80 seconds to register a patient and 15 seconds for a follow-up, lists overdue patients with high-risk ones first, and offers one-click nurse calls and automated reminders [D3-05-F03]. Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up [D3-05-F06].

For patients who keep coming, the protocol works. In Punjab and Maharashtra, 70% and 76% of patients seen again were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg alone, and 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04]. Across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82%; about 43% of starters are missing from that count [D1-06-F04]. The drugs are cheap: using amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year. Neither figure includes staff, and a full cost was not found [D3-05-F05].

OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor (chapter 1.3).

#### Who changes the dose in practice

The refill rule in chapter 1.3 sends uncontrolled patients to a doctor. Two further readings are from search summaries only. State protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose; once pressure is controlled, the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) at the health and wellness centre or sub-centre measures it and gives a month's medicines [D3-05-F31]. The duties of a CHO (community health officer) are screening, referral and follow-up, and starting treatment sits with the medical officer and staff nurse [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13]. The national NCD guidelines for 2023-2030 could not be opened, and whether a nurse or health officer may change a dose in law is open (chapter 2.6). OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.

#### Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme

Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam brings screening and medicines to the home. Launched in August 2021, it reported 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries by August 2024, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14]. Women health volunteers deliver drugs to registered patients over 45 or with poor mobility (search summary only) [D3-05-F16]. It refills; it does not step: no source says the dose is changed at the door [D3-05-F15]. OUR VIEW: the drugs already reach the door at the same dose; high treatment with low control (chapter 1.2) is the gap a dose step addresses.

#### Programmes outside India

| Programme, size | Who steps the dose | Also in the package | Result | Comparison group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| China rural project (CRHCP) | Village doctors by protocol, physician-supervised | Free or discounted drugs; doctors paid on control rate; audit; free home cuffs (search summary only) [D3-05-F21] | Chapter 2.1 | Yes, cluster trial |
| Lesotho; 103 villages, 547 people | Lay village health workers, by app | One fixed-dose pill | Under 140/90 at 12 months 58% against 48%, p=0.046 [D3-05-F24] | Yes, cluster trial against referral to a facility |
| IMPACT-BP, South Africa; 774 people | Nurses, remotely by app (not stated explicitly) | A health worker collects readings at home and delivers medicine; home cuff | Systolic 7.9-9.1 mmHg lower at 6 months [D3-05-F27] | Yes, against standard care |
| Nigeria; 60 centres, 21,922 people | Health workers under standing orders (search summary only) | Free drugs, then a US$1.60 co-pay a month; single pills rose from 16.3% to 65.2% of prescriptions and 30-day stock from 27% to 96% of centres | Control 21.7% to 55.9% (2020-2023) [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F23] | No |
| COBRA-BPS, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka; 30 rural communities, 2,645 people | Trained physicians; government health workers monitored and referred | Home visits, counselling, coordinated public care | Over 24 months, systolic fell 9.0 against 3.9 mmHg, a difference of 5.2; control 53.2% against 43.7% [D1-01-F37] | Yes, cluster trial |
| CARRS, India and Pakistan; 1,146 people with diabetes | Physicians, with software prompts | Care coordinators calling monthly; low-cost generics | Combined target 18.2% against 8.7% at 28 months, with more mild lows [D3-05-F18] (another note gives 8.1% for the comparison arm [D2-03-F14]); the chance of improving sugar, pressure and cholesterol together doubled, risk ratio 2.1 at 12 months [D1-01-F23] | Yes, randomised |
| Uganda HIV clinic; 1,082 people | Clinic | 3-month refills once controlled | Control 73.5% to 78.3%; 96.4% retained [D3-05-F36] | No |

OUR VIEW: the largest gains in control came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing. In CARRS the extra ingredient was a person following patients up.

#### What these programmes changed that software alone could not

- Drug stock: Nigeria, IHCI and China [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F02, D1-01-F38].
- Authority for a non-doctor to change drugs: China, Lesotho, and the PAHO HEARTS roadmap across 33 countries, which names nurse dose adjustment [D1-01-F09, D3-05-F24, D3-05-F28].
- A person carrying medicine to the home: IMPACT-BP and Tamil Nadu [D3-05-F27, D3-05-F14].
- Pay linked to control, and physician audit: China [D3-05-F21].
- A person who phones and books visits: CARRS and the IHCI nurses [D3-05-F18, D3-05-F03].
- Software alone, in mWellcare, added nothing [D1-01-F46].

OUR VIEW: software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.

### 2.3 What the technology can and cannot do

> **In short.**
> - A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as posture; trusting it is the hard engineering.
> - Every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing.
> - Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol; they can read and speak, but should not decide.
> - Learning each patient's response is later work: no open data or simulator exists for blood-pressure drugs.

If changing the treatment is what works, the technology questions narrow to two: can a home reading be trusted, and can a decision be kept within safe bounds. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.

#### Trusting a home reading

The American and European hypertension societies publish rules for home readings: how long to rest, how many readings to take, over how many days, and a lower threshold at home than in clinic. Chapter 4.3 applies them [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Small mistakes move the number:

| Mistake | Effect, systolic / diastolic (mmHg) |
|---|---|
| Arm on the lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover trial, 133 people, Baltimore) [D2-02-F16] |
| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) |
| Back not supported | +5 to +15 / +6 (American Heart Association) [D2-02-F18] |
| Legs crossed | +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 (same source) |
| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large one | +4.8 systolic (randomised crossover trial, 195 people) [D2-02-F19] |
| Regular cuff on an arm that needs an extra-large one | +19.5 systolic (same trial) |

Noise has already hurt an Indian trial. SMARThealth India (a stepped-wedge cluster trial, in which clusters switch on in turn; 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].

Getting the number in is also a problem. No cuff sold in India was confirmed to use the standard Bluetooth blood-pressure service [D2-02-F3], and two Omron Connect models are encrypted [D1-06-F07]. Reading a photo of the cuff's screen works in tests: a purpose-trained reader reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images and 0.9/0.5 mmHg on 1,934 Guatemalan recordings, against 4.1/2.7 mmHg for human transcribers on the Guatemalan set. But 82% of 7,205 images in another Guatemalan set were poor quality, errors sat in the last digit, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8]. A Bluetooth home cuff, the Omron HEM-7156T, costs about ₹2,600 (2026 listings ₹2,593-3,500; search summary only) [D1-06-F31].

Cuffless blood pressure is not ready. The FDA cleared the Aktiia G0 cuffless monitor on 2 Jul 2025 [D2-02-F23], but the European Society of Hypertension says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25]. OUR VIEW: cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, so dose decisions stay on cuff readings.

OUR VIEW: blood pressure is the one signal a household can measure with a validated, cheap device. A photo reaches any cuff, so the loop need not depend on Bluetooth, but every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.

#### Algorithms that set a dose

Four families of dose algorithm are in use, and each is bounded.

- **Closed-loop insulin, the model case.** Control-IQ (randomised 2:1, 168 people with type 1 diabetes, US, 6 months, against a sensor-augmented pump) raised time in range (the share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL) by 11 points and cut HbA1c by 0.33, with one ketoacidosis case [D1-01-F24]. The do-it-yourself system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down: it acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate"; and missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan [D2-03-F46].
- **Insulin titration rules.** The American Diabetes Association's 2025 rule starts basal insulin at 10 units a day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, steps it every 3 days towards a fasting target, and lowers it by 10-20% after a low with no clear reason [D1-06-F16]. India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17].
- **Blood-pressure ladders.** Fixed steps with a 30-day review, lab and pregnancy guards, and referral at the end (chapter 4.1) [D1-06-F14]. People do differ: PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if the drug were chosen per person [D2-03-F12]. A one-time "responder" label from a short run-in did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13].
- **Warfarin tables.** Feedback tables agree on no change at INR 2.0-3.0 but differ outside it (search summary only) [D1-06-F37].

OUR VIEW: every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing. A ladder is the simplest case. PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.

#### A protocol as data, and decision support in India

A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch and swapped without changing the engine. Standards exist, but none fits as it is. WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit; the blood-pressure kit is for pregnancy only and its machine-readable layers are "not yet available" [D2-03-F50]. HL7 CQL is a standard logic language whose open engine is "not a complete implementation" [D2-03-F52]. CDS Hooks returns suggestion cards with an accept button [D2-03-F53]. Testing is the hard part: when the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support, 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].

Indian trials of decision support for clinicians show where software helps.

| Trial | Design | Result |
|---|---|---|
| CARRS | Chapter 2.2 | Positive, with care coordinators |
| mWellcare | Chapter 2.1 [D2-03-F15] | Null |
| SMARThealth India | Health-worker tablet plus doctor decision support, against usual care (above) | Null on blood pressure |
| mPower Heart, Himachal Pradesh, 6,797 people | Phone tool drafts a prescription and a physician vets it; before and after, no control | Systolic -14.6 mmHg, uncontrolled [D2-03-F16] |
| IMPACT Diabetes, 418 people, 9 months | Cluster randomised; ASHAs (village health workers) with a tablet tool under physician supervision, against usual care | HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3%; physician visits 85.0% against 29.8% [D2-03-F18, D3-04-F17] |

OUR VIEW: decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so an engine must act between visits, not prompt during them. ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only on hand-written ones.

#### What language models may and may not do with doses

Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol. GPT-4, prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol on 300 simulated cases, made 13.9% "sentinel errors" in its first version; with stronger constraints and output checks the rate fell to 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs were not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) [D2-03-F38]. ChatGPT and Gemini, asked about anticoagulant hold times in 25 cases, gave "potentially dangerous recommendations in 12-20% of scenarios" [D2-03-F39]. No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44]. Of the health models the large labs have built, only MedGemma, PaPaGei and HealthBench can be downloaded, and none sets doses [D2-03-F32, D2-03-F28, D2-03-F33].

The design pattern that follows (OUR VIEW, from [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]):

1. The model handles language only: cuff photo to strict data, translation, speech.
2. A fixed, tested engine makes every decision, from the protocol file.
3. Code checks every output against the protocol: plausible ranges, two agreeing reads, a regimen that exists in the file.
4. A clinician approves every change.

For Indian languages, Sarvam's API offers speech-to-text at ₹0.49 a minute (price page, 13 Nov 2026) or ₹1.5 a minute (another listing, search summary only) [D2-03-F58, D1-06-F35]; AI4Bharat's IndicTrans2 translates 22 languages plus English under an MIT licence [D2-03-F59]; the government's Bhashini price was NOT FOUND [D2-03-F57].

#### Later work: adaptive nudging, personal response models and open data

Adaptive nudging learns when and what to send each person. In HeartSteps V1 (micro-randomised, 44 US adults, 6 weeks), any suggestion added 35 steps in 30 minutes (p = .06), fading over time [D2-03-F02]. In DIAMANTE (randomised, 168 people with diabetes and depression, US safety-net clinics, 6 months), learned text messages raised steps 19% against 1.6% for random texts and 3.9% for a weekly message; HbA1c was not in the abstract [D2-03-F10]. OUR VIEW: adaptive timing has one head-to-head win, on steps, not on a clinical measure.

A "digital twin" here is a model of one person that predicts their response to food or treatment. In a secondary analysis of an Indian randomised trial by Twin Health (319 people with type 2 diabetes, company-linked, only 59 on blood-pressure drugs), home readings guided blood-pressure drug changes and systolic fell 7.6 against 3.2 mmHg at one year; the drug changes followed a protocol, and the machine learning predicted diet response [D2-03-F19, D1-01-F20].

No open model of response to blood-pressure drugs, no open blood-pressure titration simulator, no open type 2 diabetes simulator and no large open dataset of home readings with medicine changes was found [D1-06-F42, D1-06-F43, D1-06-F30]. What exists for testing tonight: the IHCI control-by-step figures (an open-licence paper) [D1-06-F04], the R `bp` package of home blood-pressure series from Ghanaian patients and children (GPL-3) [D2-03-F61], and ShanghaiT2DM, 100 type 2 patients with glucose sensor and insulin doses over 3-14 days [D1-06-F11]. OUR VIEW: each approved step in a loop gives one labelled example (readings before, readings 30 days after), the dataset a response model would need.

### 2.4 Who is already doing this

> **In short.**
> - In India, many programmes coach around a sensor; the one product found that changes a dose is a drug maker's insulin app of unknown status.
> - Abroad, lasting businesses are paid by employers, insurers or health systems, or sell a device that delivers the dose.
> - The nearest relatives of a home dose loop are a US company whose software is in a regulator's pilot, a UK company now wound up, and a Japanese cuff maker's UK tool.
> - Most money abroad goes to products that show data or coach; no funded home blood-pressure dose-step service was found.

#### The nearest relatives

No funded startup of 2025 or 2026 was found whose funding page describes home blood-pressure dose steps by protocol. The nearest are these.

- **Cadence (US).** Remote vital signs for older adults between visits; supervised AI agents flag risk and support medicine changes under the partner medical group's protocols, and health systems pay; how far the AI decides alone is not stated. It raised a $100M Series C in June 2026, led by Spark Capital [D2-06-F1], and reports 100,000+ active patients and blood-pressure control up 70% relative (THEIR CLAIM, Jun 2026) [D2-06-F2]. On 13 Aug 2026 it said its HypertensionOS, prescription software for clinician-supervised, protocol-bound titration of blood-pressure medicines, was selected for the FDA's TEMPO pilot, which "does not constitute FDA approval or clearance" (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F31]. PHTI had named Cadence among the programmes where a team adjusts medicine [D1-05-F1].
- **Closed Loop Medicine (UK).** Its one blood-pressure trial (published 2024, company and university authors) adjusted amlodipine through an app in 205 adults over 14 weeks, with no comparison group; systolic fell 11 mmHg [D3-06-F09]. It later showed clinicians dose options for GLP-1 medicines (WeDosify, US launch 18 Sep 2025) [D2-06-F24]. The company has been in members' voluntary liquidation (a solvent winding-up by shareholders) since 28 Apr 2026 [D3-06-F07], and its website now points to a firm that licenses its patents and dosing models (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F08].
- **Omron (Japan), in the UK.** The cuff maker's Hypertension Plus (later Viso) collates home readings and drafts a medication plan that the clinician accepts or modifies (search summary only; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F35].
- **Others.** Story Health's VITAL-HF randomised 178 heart-failure patients in seven US health systems against usual care; at 6 months medicine use improved with no rise in admissions (funded by Innovaccer) [D1-05-F61]. 9amHealth's virtual specialists and pharmacists manage medicines, with a $26M Series B in May 2026; who changes doses is not stated [D2-06-F22].

#### Prescribed apps in Germany, Japan and Korea

Germany is the one country with years of numbers on apps that doctors prescribe and public insurers pay for (called DiGA). About 1.9 million were prescribed in 2020-2025, and 82% were used [D1-05-F27]. Insurers paid about EUR 400M in five years, Oviva the largest at EUR 101.9M [D1-05-F28], at an average negotiated price of EUR 227 across 40 apps [D1-05-F29]. In Japan, CureApp HT has been covered by insurance since 1 Sep 2022 [D1-05-F33]; prescription counts were NOT FOUND [D1-05-F36]. Korea approved two insomnia apps in 2023 with three-year temporary payment registration; fees and uptake were NOT FOUND [D1-05-F37, D1-05-F38]. OUR VIEW: public payers will pay for prescribed apps, but increasingly for results.

#### What funds abroad are backing

A table of 32 companies funded or launched abroad, mostly in 2025-2026, shows where the money goes. The largest rounds went to Function ($298M), Hippocratic AI ($126M), Cadence and Nourish ($100M each), and only Cadence describes medicine changes [D2-06-F42, D2-06-F20, D2-06-F5]. Blood-pressure money buys sensors, not decisions: Biobeat, Aktiia and Vital Signals raised $50M, $42M and $15M+ for products that only show readings [D2-06-F36, D2-06-F37, D2-06-F38]. Only three of the 32 rows are clearly at depth 4 (Cadence, Twin Health and WeDosify). The frontier AI labs launched consumer health features in 2026, among them ChatGPT Health (7 Jan) and Claude's health connectors (11 Jan); they read phone health data, change no treatment, and their Indian availability was NOT FOUND [D2-06-F15, D2-06-F16]. The funds name the goal but not the mechanism: an a16z essay of 3 Nov 2026 says "The opportunity is helping people act on them" [D2-06-F50], and none of the fund lines read mentions dose titration by rule.

#### The gap

OUR VIEW. No Indian service was found that turns home readings into a medicine change between visits (chapter 1.5). Abroad the space is held by US programmes paid by US payers, and the low-income-country programmes found are protocol care, not device-linked dose loops [D1-05-F65]. The pattern exists abroad inside broad virtual clinics and for weight-loss medicines, but nobody funded sells it as a blood-pressure product for a public programme run by health workers. These are one night's search results: a hospital, drug maker or state may run something unpublished.

### 2.5 The money

> **In short.**
> - Most money in blood-pressure care goes to medicines; a service priced near a pill would double the patient's bill, so usually someone else must pay.

> - On our own arithmetic the reachable Indian market is real but small for a venture fund, and the US$100 million-a-year test fails on India alone.
> - Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money; the profitable foreign ones are paid by employers and plans.

#### The US$100 million-a-year test

US$100 million a year is ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026). At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients (52,71,253). The serviceable market holds 41.9 lakh. **On this model the test fails in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (all OUR ARITHMETIC). At higher prices fewer patients are needed: 7,85,417 at ₹1,000 a month, 3,92,708 at ₹2,000, and 3,40,136 at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month [D2-05-F23]. The rest would have to come from more protocols on the same loop, a paid public tier, other countries that use the same family of protocols, or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.

| ₹299 | ₹1,504 crore | ₹35.9 crore | 26.3 lakh |

A public tier, shown apart: 420.1 lakh patients on treatment in the public programme [D1-03-F14] x ₹15 a month (ASSUMPTION) x 12 = ₹756 crore a year (OUR ARITHMETIC). A state would pay this only for results.

OUR VIEW: blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company. Price moves the result as much as clinic count does.

#### Unit economics, per patient a month

Every cost line is an ASSUMPTION from the build note, to be checked.

| Line | Value |
|---|---|
| Price to the clinic, private tier | ₹149 per active patient (ASSUMPTION), below Sugar.fit's ₹2,499 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹29,990 / 12) |
| Messages | ₹15 (WhatsApp templates; Telegram costs nothing). Two resellers copying Meta's India card give ₹0.115 a utility message and ₹0.8631 a marketing message, before 18% GST, from 1 Oct 2026 (third party, not Meta) [D3-07-F20, D3-07-F21] |
| Cloud and storage | ₹5 |
| Reading cuff photos | ₹2 (about 30 photos) |
| Health-worker call to silent patients | ₹30 (one 5-minute call a month) |
| Doctor time | 6.5-8.5 proposals per 100 patients a month at 30 seconds each, about 4 minutes per 100 patients; not costed (OUR SIMULATION and ASSUMPTION) |
| **Gross margin** | **₹149 - (15 + 5 + 2 + 30) = ₹97, about 65% (OUR ARITHMETIC)** |

OUR VIEW: the health-worker call is the largest cost, and the margin holds only if doctors approve proposals without being paid per approval.

#### What comparable companies earn and are worth

| Company | Revenue and result | Funding, value or exit |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar.fit (India) | FY25 ₹66.5 crore (+77%), loss ₹42 crore [D2-05-F19] | Not in these notes |
| Healthify (India) | FY23 ₹228.76 crore, loss ₹142 crore; FY24 about ₹206.3 crore, loss about ₹88 crore (aggregators) [D2-05-F22] | US$20M Series D, Oct 2024 |
| Omada (US) | Revenue per member US$294 a year, about US$24.5 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: 294 / 12); gross margin 76%; net income US$6.551M in Q3 2026 [D2-05-F23, D1-05-F12] | Listed |
| Twin Health (US) | Revenue NOT FOUND | US$53M Series E at about US$950M (Aug 2025) [D2-05-F15, D1-05-F48] |

No US medicine-adjusting programme publishes a price per member a month. On cost-effectiveness, a 35-year model of TASMINH2 (UK, self-titration against usual care, 2014) gave about £1,624 per QALY (a year of life in full health) for men and £4,923 for women, if the blood-pressure gain lasts 2 years for men and 5 for women (SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D2-05-F25]; no Indian study was found.

The funding climate is warm abroad and thin in Indian health. US digital health raised US$7.4 billion in 244 deals in H1 2026, against US$6.4 billion in H1 2025, with deals of US$100 million or more taking 45% [D2-05-F16]. Indian health-tech raised US$310 million in H1 2026 (headline only, tracker not named) [D2-05-F11], out of US$7.2 billion for all Indian tech start-ups (search summary only) [D2-05-F13].

OUR VIEW: about US$24.5 of revenue a member a month is reached abroad only with employer and insurer payers. Indian comparables are small, loss-making and sold at undisclosed prices.

### 2.6 The rules

> **In short.**
> - India's July 2026 guidance treats software that guides treatment as a medical device; a doctor-approved dose proposal could fall in Class A, B or C, which the regulator confirms.
> - In telemedicine, only a registered doctor may prescribe, and must deliver the prescription directly.
> - A study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first.
> - Abroad, each country pays through a clinician, and Germany ties part of the price to results.

These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO, India's medical-device regulator.

#### Software as a medical device

CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. India has four risk classes, A lowest and D highest, and the class follows the intended use, as stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. Its grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:

| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | D | C | B |
| Serious | C | B | A |
| Non-serious | B | A | A |

"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal that a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", and Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits [D2-04-F05], and a patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical". CDSCO names a hypertension digital-therapeutics platform and a Bluetooth cuff app as medical device software, and bars the wellness carve-out once a disease is named [D2-04-F07, D2-04-F09]. Unlike the US, India has no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. OUR VIEW: clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.

#### Testing on patients

A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14], which the flowchart says is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. Whether a pilot in which software drafts and a doctor decides counts as a clinical investigation is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Trials must be registered on CTRI before the first patient, with ethics approval uploaded (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]. Fees and processing days were NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].

#### Who may prescribe and change a dose

The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; such tools may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. A follow-up, under the same guidelines, means the same doctor and the same condition within 6 months of the last in-person consultation [D2-04-F17, D2-01-F10]. Whether later rules changed this in 2026 was not checked. In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription", and no law, rule or ministry order was found that lets a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18].

The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats conditions in its Schedule, which lists "Diabetes", "Heart diseases" and "High or low blood pressure"; whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested [D2-04-F31].

#### What tonight's prototype may and may not say

OUR VIEW, drawn from the rules above:
- It is a prototype for test and demonstration, not a medical device on sale and not tested on patients.
- It uses open data, simulated patients or teammates' readings, and no patient data.
- A clinician approves every dose change and directly delivers the prescription; the software only drafts and shows its reasons.
- It makes no claim that it treats or controls high blood pressure, and no claim of benefit to patients.

#### Rules and payment abroad

| Country | Device rule | How it is paid |
|---|---|---|
| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k), for example My Dose Coach and d-Nav [D2-04-F24]. Software that supports a clinician who can review its basis, and does not analyse a device signal, is not a device; whether home cuff readings count as a signal is a question for counsel [D2-04-F22, D2-04-F23] | Medicare remote monitoring needs a face-to-face initiating visit from 1 Jan 2027 [D2-04-F26] |
| Germany | The DiGA route requires a positive care effect, with a decision in 3 months [D2-04-F28] | Price negotiated after year one; from 1 Jan 2026 at least 20% of the price must depend on measured outcomes [D2-04-F29, D1-05-F31] |
| Japan | CureApp HT, approved in April 2022, has been insured since 1 Sep 2022 as an add-on app that coaches lifestyle (salt, weight, exercise), not a dose change [D3-06-F19, D2-04-F37] | From 1 Jun 2026, 90 points a month in person or 78 online, plus 7,010 yen for the app (company release and a news report); the patient pays 30% (search summary only) [D2-04-F43, D3-06-F20]. Older figures differ: 7,010 yen (Jan 2024) or about 2,490 yen a month at a 30% patient share (2022), on different bases, unreconciled [D1-05-F33]; about 8,000 yen (search summary only) [D1-01-F57] |

OUR VIEW: all three pay through a clinician, and Germany now ties part of the price to outcomes.

Full detail: Appendix B (the clinical evidence and the programmes), Appendix C (the technology), Appendix D (every player) and Appendix E (money and rules).

OUR VIEW: the research points one way. The treatment change, made by someone allowed to make it, is what works; India's programme has everything for it except a decision between visits; the technology to trust a home reading and bound a decision exists in open parts; nobody in India sells it; and nobody yet pays for it. The next chapter puts these findings together and weighs what to build.

input.content:
## 2. What the research found

Chapter 1 showed a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that stops before the dose. This chapter condenses what the research found, in plain words. It starts with the clinical evidence on what actually improves outcomes, then turns to how others have scaled care without specialists, what the technology can and cannot do, who is already doing this, where the money is and what the rules allow.

### 2.1 What actually improves outcomes

> **In short.**
> - Outcomes improved when a home reading led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when the reading was only shown or turned into a reminder.
> - Who was allowed to change the dose mattered more than the electronics.
> - Raising adherence on its own did not move outcomes.
> - The same pattern holds in diabetes, heart failure, warfarin and asthma, and the known harms of dose stepping can be met with stop rules.

The trials sort into five rules. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.

**Rule 1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring of blood pressure alone lowered systolic pressure (the upper number, in mmHg, millimetres of mercury) by 1.0 mmHg against usual care: no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, it fell 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05]. Where the dose itself moved, the falls were larger. In the UK trial TASMIN-SR (552 high-risk patients, randomised, meaning people got each treatment by chance), patients stepping their own dose by an agreed plan had systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg lower than under usual care at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. In the US trial HyperLink (450 patients, 16 clinics randomised as clusters, meaning whole clinics rather than single patients), pharmacists adjusting drugs from home readings got 57.2% controlled against 30.0% with usual care [D1-01-F04]. An independent US review by the Peterson Health Technology Institute (PHTI, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful" and programmes where care teams adjust drugs "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg fall in systolic pressure [D1-01-F39].

![Extra fall in systolic pressure against usual care, by what was done with the reading](adaptive-care-pictures/20-what-lowers-pressure.png)

*Chart: separate trials with different patients and end points, so compare the groups, not single bars [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F05, D1-01-F06, D1-01-F07].*

**Rule 2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In the UK trial TASMINH4 (1,182 patients, 12 months), the family doctor adjusted doses in every arm, and sending home readings electronically instead of on paper added 1.2 mmHg, not significant (small enough to be chance) [D1-01-F03]. In rural China, the China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP: 326 villages, 33,995 people aged 40 and over) let village doctors start and step drugs by a standard protocol under physician supervision. At 18 months, 57.0% were under 130/80 against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. After a median of 4 years, cardiovascular events were lower, with a hazard ratio (a risk ratio over time; below 1 means fewer events) of 0.75 at age 60 and over and 0.64 under 60. The programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates, so the effect cannot be credited to the protocol alone [D1-01-F38].

India has the null result that belongs here. mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps during visits. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run protocol programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: the app did not act on home readings or reach patients who never came back, and no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a dose protocol was found (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).

![Share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose](adaptive-care-pictures/21-share-controlled.png)

*Chart: three settings where someone other than a specialist was allowed to step the dose. The China programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results; the India figures are before and after among the 51% who returned, with no comparison group [D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09, D1-03-F10].*

**Rule 3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (ASCENT, 23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children raised adherence to 84% against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. A blood-pressure reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 US adults, 12 weeks) moved systolic pressure by 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.

**Rule 4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Chapter 1.5 told this side: apps and sensors sold on their own failed, while the firms that lasted are paid by employers and insurers, or sell a device that delivers the therapy.

**Rule 5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In eight remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants), median retention was 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, and payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.

#### What the loop changes, by kind

| What the loop changes | Home signal | How fast | Proof | Who decides |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (a blood test of clotting time), weight | Days to weeks: insulin every 3 days in a 2025 US rule [D1-06-F16]; blood pressure re-checked at 30 days [D1-06-F14] | Strong | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker |
| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Each meal [D1-01-F22] | Mixed | App, coach |
| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Each session [D1-06-F36] | Matches in-person care | Therapist or app |
| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Automatic | Strong | Algorithm, within limits a clinician sets [D1-05-F41] |
| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | During practice [D1-02-F15] | Weak | Patient |

OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none.

| Blood pressure | Dose stepping from home readings by the patient, a pharmacist or a village doctor (rules 1 and 2) | Strongest: up to hard outcomes at 4 years | Leg swelling 32% against 22% with self-titration in TASMINH2 [D1-01-F01]; the China gain came with free drugs and incentives |

Telemonitoring without a mandated dose protocol was null in two US trials (1,653 and 1,437 patients) [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33] |

**Prescription apps.** Software sold as a prescribed treatment has passed trials, yet most of the companies behind it failed (chapter 1.5), and the research note records that none of the prescription apps it lists changes a drug dose. The closest to this topic is Japan's CureApp HT, a lifestyle-coaching app with no drug change: in 390 untreated adults (12 sites, 12 weeks) it lowered 24-hour systolic pressure 2.4 mmHg more than lifestyle advice alone [D1-01-F07]. OUR VIEW: about half the effect of the dose-stepping trials, in patients not yet on drugs.

**Safety.** OUR VIEW: dose stepping by protocol has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. At 4 years in rural China, injurious falls, symptomatic low blood pressure, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups [D1-01-F38], and insulin-dose proposals in TeleDiab-2 (191 adults starting long-acting insulin, 4 months) caused no severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The known costs are more minor side effects, leg swelling and low blood sugar, so each needs its own safety branch.

### 2.2 How care has been scaled without specialists

> **In short.**
> - India's programme already has a protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list; the dose step still waits for a doctor's visit.
> - Patients who keep attending do well on the protocol; the loss is among those who stop coming.
> - Abroad, the largest gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill.
> - Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.

Chapter 2.1 showed that changing the dose works. This section asks how it has been delivered at scale without specialists.

#### India's hypertension programme in practice

IHCI runs a state protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first (chapter 4.1 gives one state's steps); Punjab and Maharashtra order the steps differently at the second step [D3-05-F01, D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]. Drugs are free, as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres to district hospitals [D3-05-F02]. The open-source Simple app takes about 80 seconds to register a patient and 15 seconds for a follow-up, lists overdue patients with high-risk ones first, and offers one-click nurse calls and automated reminders [D3-05-F03]. Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up [D3-05-F06].

For patients who keep coming, the protocol works. In Punjab and Maharashtra, 70% and 76% of patients seen again were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg alone, and 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04]. Across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82%; about 43% of starters are missing from that count [D1-06-F04]. The drugs are cheap: amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year, not counting staff [D3-05-F05].

OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor (chapter 1.3).

**Who changes the dose in practice.** Besides the refill rule in chapter 1.3, two readings come from search summaries only: state protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose, and once pressure is controlled the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) measures it and gives a month's medicines [D3-05-F31]; the duties of a CHO (community health officer) are screening, referral and follow-up, while starting treatment sits with the medical officer and staff nurse [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13]. Whether a nurse or health officer may change a dose in law is open (chapter 2.6). OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.

**Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme.** Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, launched in August 2021, reported 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries by August 2024, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14]. It refills; it does not step: no source says the dose is changed at the door [D3-05-F15]. OUR VIEW: high treatment with low control (chapter 1.2) is the gap a dose step addresses.

#### Programmes outside India

| Programme, size | Who steps the dose | Also in the package | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| China rural project (CRHCP) | Village doctors by protocol, physician-supervised | Free or discounted drugs; pay on control rate; audit; free home cuffs (search summary only) [D3-05-F21] | Chapter 2.1 |
| Lesotho; 103 villages, 547 people | Lay village health workers, by app | One fixed-dose pill | Under 140/90 at 12 months 58% against 48% (cluster trial against facility referral) [D3-05-F24] |
| IMPACT-BP, South Africa; 774 people | Nurses, remotely by app (not stated explicitly) | Health worker collects readings at home and delivers medicine | Systolic 7.9-9.1 mmHg lower at 6 months against standard care [D3-05-F27] |
| Nigeria; 60 centres, 21,922 people | Health workers under standing orders (search summary only) | Free drugs, then a US$1.60 co-pay a month; single pills; steady stock | Control 21.7% to 55.9% (2020-2023), no comparison group [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F23] |
| COBRA-BPS, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka; 2,645 people | Trained physicians; health workers monitored and referred | Home visits, counselling | Systolic 5.2 mmHg lower at 24 months (cluster trial) [D1-01-F37] |

OUR VIEW: the largest gains in control came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing. In CARRS the extra ingredient was a person following patients up. What these programmes changed that software alone could not was drug stock, authority for a non-doctor to change drugs (the PAHO HEARTS roadmap across 33 countries names nurse dose adjustment [D3-05-F28]), a person carrying medicine home, pay linked to control, and a person who phones and books visits. Software alone, in mWellcare, added nothing. Software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.

### 2.3 What the technology can and cannot do

> **In short.**
> - A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff, such as posture; trusting it is the hard engineering.
> - Every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing.
> - Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol; they can read and speak, but should not decide.
> - Learning each patient's response is later work: no open data or simulator exists for blood-pressure drugs.

If changing the treatment is what works, the technology questions narrow to two: can a home reading be trusted, and can a decision be kept within safe bounds. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.

#### Trusting a home reading

The American and European hypertension societies publish rules for home readings: how long to rest, how many readings, over how many days, and a lower threshold at home than in clinic; chapter 4.3 applies them [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Small mistakes move the number:

| Mistake | Effect, systolic / diastolic (mmHg) |
|---|---|
| Arm on the lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover trial, 133 people, Baltimore) [D2-02-F16] |
| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) |
| Back not supported; legs crossed | +5 to +15 / +6; +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 (American Heart Association) [D2-02-F18] |
| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large or an extra-large one | +4.8 or +19.5 systolic (randomised crossover trial, 195 people) [D2-02-F19] |

Noise has already hurt an Indian trial. SMARThealth India (a stepped-wedge cluster trial, in which groups of patients start the programme one after another; 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].

Getting the number in is also hard. No cuff sold in India was confirmed to use the standard Bluetooth blood-pressure service [D2-02-F3], and two Omron Connect models are encrypted [D1-06-F07]. A purpose-trained reader of cuff-screen photos reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images and 0.9/0.5 mmHg on 1,934 Guatemalan recordings, against 4.1/2.7 mmHg for human transcribers; but 82% of 7,205 images in another set were poor quality, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8]. A Bluetooth home cuff, the Omron HEM-7156T, costs about ₹2,600 (2026 listings ₹2,593-3,500; search summary only) [D1-06-F31]. Cuffless blood pressure is not ready: the FDA cleared the Aktiia G0 cuffless monitor on 2 Jul 2025 [D2-02-F23], but the European Society of Hypertension says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25].

OUR VIEW: blood pressure is the one signal a household can measure with a validated, cheap device. Cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, so dose decisions stay on cuff readings, and every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.

#### Algorithms that set a dose

Every dose algorithm in use is bounded. The do-it-yourself insulin system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down: it acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate"; and missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan [D2-03-F46]. Closed-loop insulin works within such limits: Control-IQ (168 people with type 1 diabetes, US, 6 months, against a sensor-augmented pump) raised time in range (the share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL) by 11 points [D1-01-F24]. The American Diabetes Association's 2025 insulin rule steps the dose every 3 days towards a fasting target and lowers it 10-20% after an unexplained low [D1-06-F16]; India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. Blood-pressure ladders use fixed steps with a 30-day review, lab and pregnancy guards and referral at the end (chapter 4.1) [D1-06-F14].

People do differ. PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if the drug were chosen per person [D2-03-F12], while a one-time "responder" label did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13]. OUR VIEW: every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing; a ladder is the simplest case, and PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.

#### A protocol as data, and decision support in India

A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch and swapped without changing the engine. Standards exist, but none fits as it is: WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit [D2-03-F50], and the open engine for the HL7 CQL logic language is "not a complete implementation" [D2-03-F52]. Testing is the hard part: when the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support, 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].

Indian trials of decision support for clinicians are mixed. CARRS (chapter 2.2) was positive with care coordinators; mWellcare (chapter 2.1) [D2-03-F15] and SMARThealth (above) were null; mPower Heart (6,797 people, Himachal Pradesh), in which a phone tool drafts a prescription and a physician vets it, reported systolic 14.6 mmHg lower but had no control group [D2-03-F16]. IMPACT Diabetes (cluster randomised, 418 people, 9 months) gave ASHAs (village health workers) a tablet tool under physician supervision: HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3% with usual care [D2-03-F18, D3-04-F17]. OUR VIEW: decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so an engine must act between visits, not prompt during them, and ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.

#### What language models may and may not do with doses

GPT-4, prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol on 300 simulated cases, made 13.9% "sentinel errors" in its first version; with stronger constraints and output checks the rate fell to 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs were not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) [D2-03-F38]. ChatGPT and Gemini, asked about anticoagulant hold times in 25 cases, gave "potentially dangerous recommendations in 12-20% of scenarios" [D2-03-F39]. No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44]. Of the health models the large labs have built, only MedGemma, PaPaGei and HealthBench can be downloaded, and none sets doses [D2-03-F32, D2-03-F28, D2-03-F33].

OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]: the model handles language only (reading the cuff photo, translation, speech); a fixed, tested engine makes every decision from the protocol file; code checks every output against the protocol; and a clinician approves every change. For Indian languages, Sarvam's speech-to-text costs ₹0.49 a minute (price page, 13 Nov 2026) or ₹1.5 a minute (another listing, search summary only) [D2-03-F58, D1-06-F35], and AI4Bharat's IndicTrans2 translates 22 languages under an MIT licence [D2-03-F59].

#### Later work

Adaptive nudging learns when and what to send each person. In DIAMANTE (randomised, 168 people with diabetes and depression, US safety-net clinics, 6 months), learned text messages raised steps 19% against 1.6% for random texts and 3.9% for a weekly message [D2-03-F10]; OUR VIEW: one head-to-head win, on steps, not on a clinical measure. A "digital twin" (a model of one person that predicts their response) is further off: in a company-linked secondary analysis of an Indian trial by Twin Health, home readings guided blood-pressure drug changes by a protocol, with systolic 7.6 against 3.2 mmHg lower at one year, but only 59 people were on blood-pressure drugs [D2-03-F19, D1-01-F20]. No open model of response to blood-pressure drugs, no titration simulator, no open type 2 diabetes simulator and no large open dataset of home readings with medicine changes was found [D1-06-F42, D1-06-F43, D1-06-F30]. What can be tested on now is the programme's control-by-step figures [D1-06-F04] and open home blood-pressure series (the R `bp` package, GPL-3) [D2-03-F61]. OUR VIEW: each approved step in a loop gives one labelled example, readings before and 30 days after, which is the dataset a response model would need.

### 2.4 Who is already doing this

> **In short.**
> - In India, many programmes coach around a sensor; the one product found that changes a dose is a drug maker's insulin app of unknown status.
> - Abroad, lasting businesses are paid by employers, insurers or health systems, or sell a device that delivers the dose.
> - The nearest relatives of a home dose loop are a US company whose software is in a regulator's pilot, a UK company now wound up, and a Japanese cuff maker's UK tool.
> - Most money abroad goes to products that show data or coach; no funded home blood-pressure dose-step service was found.

Chapter 1.5 told why the market has not fixed the gap. This section maps who is in it, by adaptive depth.
